triage.summary:
The gap is closed. In this setting (K arms, stochastic rewards, subgaussian noise, worst-case cumulative regret), the minimax rate is Θ(√(KT)). The database's best upper bound, K^{3/4}·√T·polylog (from jin2026nearly), is much weaker than results already known.

Audibert & Bubeck (2009) introduced MOSS (Minimax Optimal Strategy in the Stochastic case), which achieves O(√(KT)) worst-case regret with no log factor. It was the first algorithm proved minimax optimal. A 2024 survey (arXiv 2412.02251) cites the bound as 39√(KT) + Σ_k Δ_k for sub-Gaussian rewards, proved via Doob's submartingale inequality. This matches the √(KT)/20 lower bound already in the database up to a constant. That closes the polynomial gap in K and the log gap in T.

Later algorithms also reach √(KT) minimax regret:
- MOSS-anytime (Degenne & Perchet 2016) removes the need to know T.
- KL-UCB++ (Ménard & Garivier 2017, arXiv 1702.07211) is minimax and asymptotically optimal, but is not anytime.
- ADA-UCB (Lattimore 2018) is minimax and asymptotically optimal.
- KL-UCB-switch (arXiv 1805.05071) is optimal from both the distribution-free and distribution-dependent viewpoints.
- MOTS (arXiv 2003.01803) is a minimax-optimal Thompson Sampling variant.

Caveat: one source notes that the asymptotic-optimality claims for KL-UCB++, AdaUCB and MOTS are stated for Gaussian or other specific families. This does not affect the minimax √(KT) rate, which MOSS achieves under subgaussian noise.

Two gaps in what I checked:
- The Lattimore–Szepesvári book's Chapter 9, "The Upper Confidence Bound Algorithm: Minimax Optimality", covers MOSS in Section 9.1; I saw this in the table of contents. I did not see its theorem text, so the constant (~39) and the 1-subgaussian assumption there come from secondary sources and memory.
- I did not fetch the original Audibert & Bubeck paper.

triage.summary: Your database's bounds are order sqrt(KT log(K/delta)) above and sqrt(KT log(1/delta)) below (Gerchinovitz & Lattimore 2016), a sqrt(log K) gap at fixed delta. A 2026 arXiv preprint (Bacchiocchi, Cesari, Colomboni, 2608.12231, v2 25 Aug 2026) proves the matching lower bound in its Theorem 2. For any algorithm, a deterministic adaptive adversary with losses in [0,1] forces P(R_T >= c*sqrt(dT(log C(d,m) + log(1/delta)))) >= delta. This holds for delta <= delta_0 (a universal constant whose value the paper does not give) and T above a threshold polynomial in d, m and log(1/delta). With m=1 this is Omega(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))). The authors say this closes the remaining log K gap left by Gerchinovitz & Lattimore. Their algorithm's upper bound, O(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))), matches EXP3-KW, so the bound is tight up to constants. Caveats: (1) the lower bound needs an adaptive (non-anticipating) adversary, and the paper does not settle the oblivious case, where the only known lower bound remains sqrt(KT log(1/delta)); (2) the result is for confidence-tuned algorithms (delta fixed in advance); (3) it is a single, very recent preprint, not peer reviewed as far as I can tell. Gerchinovitz & Lattimore themselves (full text read) do not mention the log K gap or call it open. I tried to check Audibert & Bubeck's JMLR 2010 and COLT 2009 PDFs for a high-probability bound without log K under oblivious adversaries, but neither PDF rendered, so that question is unchecked.

With m=1 this gives Omega(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))), which the authors say closes the log K gap left by Gerchinovitz & Lattimore. Their matching upper bound is O(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))) against adaptive adversaries, the same as EXP3-KW.

papers.claim: Exp3-IX high-probability upper bound (the database's best upper bound).

triage.summary:
The gap has two parts, and only the log T part closes.

1. **T-direction (closes).** The extra log T in the database's upper bounds comes from setting delta=1/T in high-probability bounds. Exp4 (Auer et al. 2002) gets expected regret O(sqrt(KT log N)) even against adversaries, so it also holds for stochastic contexts. Kale's bound O(sqrt(KT log(N/K))) is better still. With this, the T-dependence is Theta(sqrt(T)). Caveat: I saw these two bounds only as summarised in the Chase et al. and Ito papers. I did not fetch the Exp4 or Kale papers themselves.

2. **K-direction (still open for this setting).** What remains is a factor of about log K between the upper bound sqrt(KT log(N/K)) and the lower bound sqrt(KT log N / log K) (Agarwal et al. 2012; Seldin & Lugosi 2016). Ito (NeurIPS 2024) states this exact gap. He proves a matching Omega(sqrt(KT log(N/K))) lower bound only for a modified protocol where the learner picks an expert before seeing the advice, which is not the standard setting.

   Chase, Ito & Mehalel (arXiv 2511.00257; COLT 2026) do close the gap, giving Theta(sqrt(TK log(N/K))). However, their hard instance uses an adaptive adversary: the advice is redrawn based on the learner's pulls. So it does not apply to i.i.d. stochastic contexts with Bernoulli rewards. The authors themselves only conjecture that the bound holds for oblivious adversaries.

Because a stochastic i.i.d. instance is a special case of an oblivious one, the tight bound for stochastic contexts with Bernoulli rewards is unproven. That makes it a known open (conjectured) problem rather than a closed one.

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00257 , https://proceedings.mlr.press/v336/chase26a.html , https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/7169e48889a07662f4168e3911c4a69e-Abstract.html

The hard instance redraws advice based on the learner's pulls. The authors only conjecture the bound holds for oblivious adversaries, so it does not cover i.i.d. stochastic contexts. triage.summary:
The T-dependence gap is mostly an artifact of how the database states its upper bounds. Its entries are high-probability bounds with delta=1/T, which brings in log(NT). Bounds on expected regret avoid this. Kale (2014) gives O(sqrt(KT log(N/K))), which Chase, Ito & Mehalel cite as the matching upper bound. That bound is proved for non-stochastic expert advice, so it should also hold when contexts are i.i.d., which is a special case.

The K-dependence gap is the real one. The lower bound is sqrt(KT log N / log K), from Agarwal et al. 2012 and Seldin & Lugosi. The upper bound is sqrt(KT log(N/K)). Recent work closed this gap, but only outside the stochastic-context setting:
- Cesa-Bianchi, Eldowa, Esposito & Olkhovskaya (arXiv 2406.16802) prove Omega(sqrt(KT ln(N/K))), but only under a restricted feedback model.
- Ito (NeurIPS 2024) proves the same lower bound for a different protocol, where the player commits to an expert before seeing the advice.
- Chase, Ito & Mehalel (arXiv 2511.00257, COLT 2026) settle the minimax rate for the standard non-stochastic problem at Theta(sqrt(TK log(N/K))). Their hard instance uses an adaptive adversary: advice for a batch of arms is redrawn only after the learner pulls an arm from that batch, so advice is not i.i.d. across rounds. The authors only conjecture that the bound also holds against an oblivious adversary.

None of these lower bounds covers stochastic i.i.d. contexts with i.i.d. rewards, which is the setting asked about. I found no paper that removes the 1/log K factor there. The authors' stated conjecture marks the oblivious case, and by extension the stochastic case, as open.

One caveat: the Ito NeurIPS 2024 PDF did not render, so I could not check its hard instance directly. What I report about it comes from the abstract and search snippets.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed up to iterated-log factors, and the paper that closes it is the one the database already takes its lower bound from: Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019, arXiv:1904.00242).

**Setting.** Linear contextual bandits with adversarial, time-varying finite action sets of size n.

**Lower bound.** The paper proves Ω(√(dT log T log n)) for n ≤ 2^{d/2}, valid when T ≥ d(log₂ n)^{1+ε}. Taking n = 2^{d/2} recovers the database's Ω(d√(T log T)); that substitution is my own inference, the paper does not state it.

**Upper bound.** The same paper's Variable-Confidence-Level (VCL) SupLinUCB algorithm "matches the lower bound up to iterated logarithmic factors". That gives O(√(dT log T log n)·poly(log log T)), which saves two √log T factors over earlier SupLinUCB analyses. The database instead lists LinTS (Agrawal & Goyal 2013), which is much looser.

**What remains open.** Only a poly(log log T) gap. If the database insists on exact log tightness, "open_known (log log gap)" would be the stricter label.

**Caveats.**
- I read only the abstract and search summaries, not the paper's theorem statements. The explicit form √(dT log T log n)·poly(log log T) is inferred from the abstract's "matches the lower bound up to iterated logarithmic factors" and a talk abstract by Yuan Zhou.
- I didn't check whether the upper bound's analysis needs any extra assumption beyond this setting, e.g. knowing σ.

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00242 ; https://proceedings.mlr.press/v99/li19b.html ; https://itcs.sufe.edu.cn/41/5b/c10453a213339/page.htm

For infinite action sets, a talk abstract gives O(√(d²T log T)·poly(log log T)) against a lower bound of Ω(√(d²T log T)).

triage.summary:
I found no source that closes this gap or calls it a known open problem for this exact setting. The setting is a fixed finite action set of K points, oblivious adversary, losses in the polar of the action set, and expected regret.

The setting's upper bound is O(√(dT log K)) (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi and Kakade, 2012, Theorem 4). Its abstract presents this only as an upper bound. It calls the d√(T log T) bound for compact action sets "minimax optimal up to a logarithmic factor", but makes no such claim for the √(dT log K) bound.

The only K-dependent lower bound I confirmed for a fixed action set is for K = 2^d. Shamir (2015), in the dual normalization, proves an Ω((d−1)√T) lower bound for the hypercube [−1,1]^d (Theorem 6, which needs T ≥ d⁴/4). Because the losses are linear, this also applies to the corner set {−1,1}^d, where d√T is the same order as √(dT log K). It also cites a prior Ω(d√T) lower bound for the Boolean hypercube. Two caveats: Shamir allows sub-Gaussian loss noise rather than strictly bounded losses, and says this relaxation costs only a √log T factor in lower bounds. At K = d (the simplex), Shamir's Ω(√(dT)) lower bound matches EXP3, and no log K term appears.

So √log K is needed at the extreme K = 2^d (up to the noise-model caveat), but I found no lower bound for general K.

The most relevant candidate is Ito (NeurIPS 2024), "On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice". Its abstract states an upper bound of O(√(dT log(K·min{1, S/d}))) with a matching lower bound, where S is the number of contexts. With S = 1 this would give Θ(√(dT log(K/d))) and close the gap. However, I could not read the full text: the PDF did not extract and OpenReview was blocked by a browser check. I therefore could not confirm that the lower bound covers S = 1, nor its loss normalization or adversary model. It may need S ≥ d.

Bacchiocchi, Cesari and Colomboni (arXiv 2608.12231) prove a matching lower bound of order √(dT log(K/δ)). But it is a high-probability bound against adaptive adversaries for m-set bandits, so it does not settle the expected-regret question. Li et al. (2019), Ω(√(dT log K log T)), is for stochastic contextual bandits whose action sets change over time; I saw it only cited secondhand and did not fetch it.

The verdict is "blank" because Ito (2024) could not be checked. If its lower bound covers S = 1 under bounded polar losses, the verdict should be "closed".

triage.summary: Closed: the d·√T upper bound matches a Θ(d√T) minimax rate stated in the literature for a finite action set, the boolean hypercube {−1,+1}^d with 2^d actions. Shamir (COLT 2015, arXiv:1408.2368) normalizes losses by the dual norm of the action set, max over w in W of |⟨w,x⟩| ≤ 1. For the hypercube that is exactly the l1 ball, matching this setting. His introduction states: "When the domain W is the boolean hypercube {−1,+1}^d, the minimax optimal regret is Θ(d√T)", crediting Dani-Kakade-Hayes (NIPS 2007) and Audibert-Bubeck-Lugosi (COLT 2011). The setting has no parameter for the number of actions K, so the worst case over finite action sets is at least d√T. The database's √(dT) lower bounds come from the case K≈d. Exp2 gives √(dT log K) (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade 2012), which becomes d√T when log K≈d; their abstract also reports an efficient d√n algorithm for the hypercube. Caveats: I could not extract the PDFs of the cited source papers (Dani et al. 2007, ABL 2011) to check their exact normalization. Shamir's own Theorem 6 is for the continuous cube [−1,1]^d with Gaussian losses, not bounded ±1 losses. ABL 2014 (arXiv:1204.4710) proves m√(dn) with per-coordinate [0,1] losses, which rescales to only √(dn). A search summary reported Bubeck's blog citing Ω(d√T) for some action set (Dani et al. 2008, ABL), but I could not open the archived page to confirm it.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization
papers.claim: Introduction states that for the boolean hypercube {-1,+1}^d (finite, 2^d actions), with losses normalized so that max_w |<w,x>| <= 1 (the l1 ball for the cube), the minimax optimal regret is Theta(d sqrt T), citing Dani-Kakade-Hayes 2007 and Audibert-Bubeck-Lugosi 2011. Theorem 6 gives c(d-1)sqrt(T) for [-1,1]^d with Gaussian losses.

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback
papers.claim: Exp2 with John's exploration achieves sqrt(dn log N) for N actions with losses bounded by 1, and d sqrt(n log n) for compact sets, which is minimax optimal up to log factors without further assumptions on the action set; also an efficient d sqrt(n) algorithm for the hypercube.

papers.title: The Price of Bandit Information for Online Optimization (Dani, Hayes, Kakade)
papers.claim: Bandit algorithm with O*(n^{3/2} sqrt T) regret, plus lower bounds showing the price of bandit information is at least order n relative to the full-information rate; cited by Shamir for the Theta(d sqrt T) hypercube rate.

papers.title: Regret in Online Combinatorial Optimization (Audibert, Bubeck, Lugosi)
papers.claim: Bandit lower bound 0.02 m sqrt(dn) for a subset of {0,1}^d with per-coordinate losses in [0,1]; this does not by itself give d sqrt T under |<a,l>|<=1 normalization.

triage.summary: Closed for undirected strongly observable graphs; still open for directed ones. Upper bound: Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari and Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.15383) prove O(sqrt(alpha*T*(1+ln(K/alpha)))) with q-Tsallis FTRL. This beats the database's sqrt(alpha*T)*log(KT) and has no log T factor. Their own lower bound is Omega(sqrt(alpha*T*ln K/ln alpha)), which shows a log factor in K is necessary. Chen, He and Zhang (arXiv:2307.07264) prove Theta(sqrt(T*sum_k log(m_k+1))) for disjoint-clique (grouped-arm) feedback. The conclusion of Eldowa et al. says this implies their algorithm is worst-case optimal up to constants for every (K, alpha); I read that on the ar5iv page and did not open the Chen et al. theorem itself. So the worst-case rate is Theta(sqrt(alpha*T*(1+log(K/alpha)))), not sqrt(alpha*T). For directed strongly observable graphs, Eldowa et al. report a best known bound of about sqrt(alpha*T*(log K)^3) and call the extension considerably harder; my searches found no later paper closing it. The arXiv PDF did not extract, so these statements come from the ar5iv HTML and abstracts.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Online Learning with Feedback Graphs
papers.claim: Upper bound O(sqrt(alpha T (1+ln(K/alpha)))) for undirected strongly observable graphs using q-Tsallis FTRL. Lower bound Omega(sqrt(alpha T ln K / ln alpha)) for alpha >= 2. Conclusion says follow-up work on disjoint cliques implies worst-case optimality up to constants for each (K, alpha). Says the directed case is considerably harder, with best known about sqrt(alpha T (log K)^3).

papers.title: On Interpolating Experts and Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.claim: Minimax regret Theta(sqrt(T sum_k log(m_k+1))) when arms are partitioned into groups that reveal each other's losses (disjoint-clique feedback graphs). Gives the matching lower bound Omega(sqrt(alpha T log(K/alpha))) for worst-case graphs with given K and alpha.

triage.summary: Known bounds: the upper bound O(sqrt(KT log(K/δ))) comes from Exp3.P and Exp3-IX (Neu 2015). The lower bound Ω(sqrt(KT log(1/δ))) is Gerchinovitz & Lattimore 2016, which per Bacchiocchi et al. holds even for losses fixed in advance. The remaining gap is sqrt(log K). Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni (arXiv:2608.12231, 2026) prove a matching Θ(sqrt(dT log(K/δ))) high-probability bound for m-set bandits. For m=1 this shows log K is unavoidable for K-armed bandits, but only against ADAPTIVE non-anticipating adversaries: the lower bound uses a deterministic adaptive adversary. The paper says: "Our corollary closes this gap when the adversary is adaptive and non-anticipating." The parts of its HTML I read (main text and part of the appendices; the rest was cut off) say nothing about oblivious adversaries. I found no paper that closes the gap for oblivious adversaries and none that explicitly calls it open. I could not check whether Audibert & Bubeck's INF (JMLR 2010) or Tsallis-INF gives a log-K-free high-probability bound for oblivious adversaries, because the PDFs came back as unreadable compressed streams. So the oblivious case is unresolved from what I could verify. Bacchiocchi et al. should be added to the database for the adaptive variant.

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits (Bacchiocchi, Cesari, Colomboni)
papers.claim: High-probability regret Θ(sqrt(dT log(K/δ))) against adaptive non-anticipating adversaries. For m=1 this closes the sqrt(log K) gap left by Gerchinovitz-Lattimore, but only for adaptive adversaries; the lower bound uses a deterministic adaptive adversary.

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits (Gerchinovitz, Lattimore)
papers.claim: No strategy can get high-probability regret smaller than order sqrt(KT log(1/δ)) (Theorem 1). Per Bacchiocchi et al., this holds even for loss sequences fixed in advance (oblivious). The paper also notes that tuning without knowing δ moves log(1/δ) outside the square root.

papers.title: Explore no more: Improved high-probability regret bounds for non-stochastic bandits (Neu)
papers.claim: Exp3-IX achieves high-probability regret O(sqrt(KT log K) + sqrt(KT/log K) log(1/δ)), and O(sqrt(KT log(K/δ))) when tuned for δ.

triage.summary: Closed by a 2026 preprint, Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni (arXiv:2608.12231). Its Theorem 2 / Corollary 1, with m=1 and d=K, shows that for every policy there is a deterministic adaptive non-anticipating adversary (losses in [0,1]) such that, with probability at least δ, R_T ≥ c·√(KT(log K + log(1/δ))). This holds for δ ≤ δ₀, a universal constant the paper does not give explicitly, and for T above a threshold polynomial in K and log(1/δ). It matches the Exp3.P upper bound O(√(KT log(K/δ))) up to constants, so the √(log K) gap is closed against adaptive adversaries. The Gerchinovitz–Lattimore lower bound √(KT log(1/δ)) is for loss sequences fixed in advance (oblivious). The same paper's Theorem 1 gives a matching high-probability upper bound against adaptive adversaries, with constant around 160. Caveats: this is an arXiv preprint (v2) with no peer review seen; I read only the first 100k of about 168k characters of the HTML; and the δ range and T threshold are not explicit. The oblivious case may still have the gap, but it is outside this setting.

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits
papers.claim: For δ ≤ δ₀ and T large, every policy faces an adaptive adversary with P(R_T ≥ c√(dT(log C(d,m)) + log(1/δ)))) ≥ δ; for m=1 this is Ω(√(KT log(K/δ))), matching their high-probability upper bound C√(KT(log K + log(1/δ))) (and Exp3.P's bound).

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits
papers.claim: High-probability lower bound Ω(√(KT log(1/δ))) for oblivious (fixed in advance) loss sequences.

papers.title: Explore no more: Improved high-probability regret bounds for non-stochastic bandits
papers.claim: Exp3-IX upper bound of order √(KT log(K/δ)) with high probability.

triage.summary: I found no published result that closes this gap, and no source that names it as an open problem. Babaioff, Dughmi, Kleinberg and Slivkins (arXiv 1108.4142) prove both bounds against the fixed-price benchmark: regret O((k log n)^{2/3}) for their strategy, and Ω(k^{2/3}) for any detail-free strategy (Theorem 6.1). Here k is the supply (B) and n the number of buyers (T). The paper says the upper bound is 'best possible up to a factor of O(log n)', which acknowledges the (log T)^{2/3} gap without calling it open. Slivkins' survey (arXiv 1904.07272) calls the Õ(B^{2/3}) rate optimal, but only up to log factors. Flajolet and Jaillet (arXiv 1510.01800) model limited-supply pricing as bandits with knapsacks; the search result did not show them removing the log factor in this worst-case setting. A 2026 paper on a related but different setting (censored demand, adversarial inventory; arXiv 2609.32949) is also optimal only 'up to logarithmic factors'. So the gap appears to remain, but no source I saw calls it an open problem.

papers.title: Dynamic Pricing with Limited Supply
papers.claim: Detail-free strategy with regret O((k log n)^{2/3}) against the fixed-price benchmark; Theorem 6.1 shows o(k^{2/3}) is impossible. The paper says the upper bound is best possible up to an O(log n) factor.

papers.title: Introduction to Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.claim: Calls the Õ(B^{2/3}) rate for dynamic pricing with limited supply optimal, since the Ω(B^{2/3}) lower bound holds against the best fixed arm. Optimal only up to log factors.

papers.title: Logarithmic regret bounds for Bandits with Knapsacks
papers.claim: Models limited-supply pricing as bandits with knapsacks with two resources, time and inventory. The search result did not show it closing the worst-case log gap.

papers.title: Optimal Nonparametric Dynamic Pricing with Censored Demand and Adversarial Inventory
papers.claim: Related setting: O(PD T^{2/3} log^{1/3} T) upper bound against Ω(T^{2/3}) lower bound, described as minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors.

triage.summary: This gap appears to be openly acknowledged and still unresolved. 'bai2021sample' is Bai, Jin, Wang & Xiong, "Sample-Efficient Learning of Stackelberg Equilibria in General-Sum Games" (NeurIPS 2021, arXiv 2102.11494). The pure-exploration task in this setting is learning an approximate Stackelberg equilibrium in a linear bandit game. I fetched the ar5iv HTML version and confirmed both bounds from the paper. Theorem 5 gives an O~(d^2/eps^2) upper bound, reached by finding a (gap_eps + eps)-approximate equilibrium. The paper also gives an Omega(d/eps^2) lower bound, adapted from its bandit-game lower bound and proved in Appendix E.2. The authors themselves say the upper bound "has at most a O~(d) gap from the lower bound." Their conclusion lists "the optimal sample complexity for bandit-RL games and linear-bandit games" as a future direction. I searched for later work and found none that tightens the dependence on d. The work I did find studies different settings: "Online Learning in Stackelberg Games with an Omniscient Follower" (arXiv 2301.11518) is a regret result under a different observation model, and "The Sample Complexity of Stackelberg Games" (arXiv 2405.06977) is about general games, not feature dimension. So the d-versus-d^2 gap is known to be open, as far as these searches show. I did not identify li2023tight. The direct PDF fetches came back as binary that the tool could not read, but the ar5iv HTML worked, so the claims above come from text I actually saw.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Learning of Stackelberg Equilibria in General-Sum Games
papers.claim: For linear bandit games, Theorem 5 gives O~(d^2/eps^2) samples to find a (gap_eps+eps)-approximate Stackelberg equilibrium. The paper also proves an Omega(d/eps^2) lower bound and says the upper bound has 'at most a O~(d) gap from the lower bound.' The conclusion names the optimal sample complexity for linear-bandit games as a future direction.

triage.summary: Not closed, and I found no explicit statement that it is open. Liu, Tajdini, Wagenmaker & Wei (arXiv:2410.07533, NeurIPS 2024) improve the corruption terms: Theorem 4.1 gives O(d sqrt(T log(T/δ)) + Z log T) with Z = dC for corruption that depends on the chosen action (√d·C∞ for weak corruption). A remark gives O(sqrt(dT log(KT/δ)) + Z log T) for K arms, which replaces the C^2 term with dC log T. That bound still has log T inside the square root, so the √log T gap in T (and the √log K gap) remains. The lower bounds they cite, Ω(d√T + dC) (Bogunovic et al. 2021) and Ω(d√T + √d C∞), have no log T factor. Li-Wang-Zhou's Ω(sqrt(dT log T log n)) lower bound (arXiv:1904.00242) is for action sets that change each period, so it does not cover a fixed finite arm set. One search summary said phased elimination gets sqrt(dT log K) without log T in the uncorrupted fixed-arm case; I did not confirm this from a primary source. I found no corruption-robust result that removes log T, and no paper stating this gap as open; Liu et al.'s stated open problems cover only the adversarial and contextual settings. I read only the first half of the 2410.07533 HTML page.

papers.title: Corruption-Robust Linear Bandits: Minimax Optimality and Gap-Dependent Misspecification
papers.claim: Randomized phased elimination: O(d sqrt(T log(T/δ)) + Z log T) with Z = dC (strong) or √d C∞ (weak). A remark gives O(sqrt(dT log(KT/δ)) + Z log T) for finite K. Cites lower bounds Ω(d√T + dC) (Bogunovic et al. 2021) and Ω(d√T + √d C∞) (Lattimore et al. 2020).

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(sqrt(dT log T log n)) for n ≤ 2^{d/2} actions per period, for linear contextual bandits with action sets that change over time, so it does not apply to a fixed finite arm set.

papers.title: Nearly Optimal Algorithms for Linear Contextual Bandits with Adversarial Corruptions
papers.claim: Weighted-OFUL algorithm whose regret nearly matches lower bounds for known and unknown C, up to log factors, in linear contextual bandits under adversarial corruption.

triage.summary: The √(log K) gap is closed: the worst-case simple regret is Θ(√(K/T)) for T ≥ K. A known reduction gives the matching upper bound. Recommend arm i with probability T_i(n)/n, where T_i(n) is the number of times arm i was played. Then expected simple regret equals expected cumulative regret divided by n. I saw this reduction stated in a search snippet attributed to Bubeck, Munos & Stoltz (arXiv 0802.2655, later versions). MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck, COLT 2009) has cumulative regret O(√(KT)) with no log factor. Combining the two gives simple regret O(√(K/T)), which matches the Ω(√(K/T)) lower bound up to constants. An explicit statement of this result appears in Oki & Sakaue (arXiv 2405.12439), which I read in its HTML version. Their Prop. 4.1 and Appendix B (with M arms and T′ rounds) run MOSS and return an arm uniformly at random from those played. They bound the cumulative regret by 39√(MT′)+M, citing Lattimore–Szepesvári Thm 9.1, and get simple regret ≤ 40√(M/T′). They call this a known result. The Lattimore–Szepesvári result assumes 1-subgaussian noise, and rewards in [0,1] are 1/2-subgaussian, so it applies here. Limitations: I could not extract text from the PDFs of Bubeck et al., the Lattimore–Szepesvári book or Bubeck's thesis. My evidence for the reduction in 0802.2655 is a search snippet, not the paper text. The closing citation is the Oki–Sakaue appendix together with the MOSS paper, whose abstract I saw saying it removes the extra log factor.

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Adversarial and Stochastic Bandits (Audibert, Bubeck)
papers.claim: MOSS, a modification of UCB1, has distribution-free cumulative regret of order √(nK) in stochastic K-armed bandits, removing the extra log factor.

papers.title: Pure Exploration for Multi-Armed Bandit Problems / Pure exploration in finitely-armed and continuous-armed bandits (Bubeck, Munos, Stoltz)
papers.claim: If the forecaster recommends arm i with probability T_i(n)/n, then E r_n = E R_n / n, so cumulative-regret upper bounds become simple-regret upper bounds. With MOSS this gives O(√(K/n)). Seen in a search snippet; I could not read the PDF.

papers.title: No-Regret M♮-Concave Function Maximization: Stochastic Bandit Algorithms and Hardness of Adversarial Full-Information Setting (Oki, Sakaue)
papers.claim: Prop. 4.1 / App. B: a MOSS-based pure-exploration algorithm that returns a random arm has simple regret ≤ 40√(M/T′), with no log M factor. It uses the cumulative bound 39√(MT′)+M from Lattimore & Szepesvári Thm 9.1. The paper describes the O(T^{-1/2}) simple regret as known.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed, and it only exists because the database is missing a result. The classical minimax lower bound for K-armed adversarial bandits is of order √(KT), with no log factor. Applied to K = 2, it gives Ω(√T), which matches Exp3's O(√(T log 2)) = O(√T) upper bound up to constants. The database's best lower bound, √T/log T (Pacchiano et al. 2020), is therefore weaker than what is already known.

Sources:
- **Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund and Schapire (SIAM J. Computing 2002).** The abstract I found says their O(T^{-1/2}) per-round convergence rate is best possible, shown by a matching lower bound.
- **Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi survey (arXiv 1204.5721), Theorem 3.4 "Minimax lower bound".** It states inf over forecasters, sup over reward distributions, of regret ≥ (1/20)√(nK). The rewards are i.i.d. Bernoulli, which also makes them an oblivious adversarial sequence in [0,1]. The proof compares Bernoulli(1/2) arms against Bernoulli(1/2 + √(K/n)).

The construction works for any K ≥ 2, but I did not see the explicit "K ≥ 2" or "n ≥ K" side conditions in the text I retrieved. The PDF fetches returned unreadable binary. From the snippets alone, then, the K = 2 case is a reasonable reading of the result rather than something I saw stated outright. The (K−1)n form of the lower bound in Lattimore–Szepesvári, Section 15.2, would cover K = 2 directly, but I could not see the theorem text.

Gerchinovitz & Lattimore (2016) refine these adversarial lower bounds further. Either way, the worst-case regret for K = 2 is Θ(√T).

papers.title: The Nonstochastic Multiarmed Bandit Problem
papers.claim: By Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund and Schapire (SIAM J. Comput. 32(1):48-77). Exp3 achieves an O(T^{-1/2}) per-round convergence rate to the best arm, i.e. O(√(KT log K)) regret. A matching lower bound shows this rate is best possible, i.e. Ω(√(KT)) regret for oblivious adversaries.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems
papers.claim: Theorem 3.4 (Minimax lower bound): inf over forecasters, sup over reward distributions, of regret ≥ (1/20)√(nK). Rewards are i.i.d. Bernoulli, hence in [0,1] and a valid oblivious adversarial sequence. Taking K = 2 gives Ω(√n), matching the Exp3 upper bound up to constants.

papers.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits
papers.claim: By Gerchinovitz & Lattimore (NeurIPS 2016). Refines the minimax Ω(√(KT)) lower bounds for adversarial bandits into more detailed, data-dependent lower bounds.

triage.summary: For bandit linear optimization on the cube [-1,1]^d with losses in the l1 ball (|a^T z| <= 1), Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (2012), Theorem 5, give R_n <= 2d sqrt(3 n log 2). The same paper states that d sqrt(n) is the minimax rate for the cube, citing Dani, Hayes & Kakade (2008): "this regret is minimax optimal" (Sec. 4) and "action sets (such as the hypercube) where the minimax rate is of order d sqrt(n)" (Intro). The Dani-Hayes-Kakade abstract claims the price of bandit information is at least sqrt(n), which against sqrt(nT) full-information regret means Omega(n sqrt T) bandit regret. I could not read their PDF, so their exact theorem, decision set and constant are unverified; that the construction is the bounded-loss cube comes from the 2012 paper's citation. Shamir (2015), Theorem 6, gives c(d-1)sqrt(T) on [-1,1]^d for T >= d^4/4 with stochastic losses whose mean lies in the l1 ball and whose tails are sub-Gaussian, not bounded by 1. So the d-exponent gap (1 vs 0.5) closes at Theta(d sqrt T); the database is missing the Omega(d sqrt T) lower bound.

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Kakade)
papers.claim: Theorem 5: for A = {||x||_inf <= 1} and Z = {||z||_1 <= 1}, OSMD gives R_n <= 2d sqrt(3 n log 2). The paper says this is minimax optimal by Dani et al. 2008 ('there exists action sets (such as the hypercube) where the minimax rate is of order d sqrt(n)').

papers.title: The Price of Bandit Information for Online Optimization (Dani, Hayes, Kakade)
papers.claim: NeurIPS 2007 (vol. 20, printed 2008). Abstract: the gap between bandit and full-information regret is at least sqrt(n), i.e. an Omega(n sqrt T) bandit lower bound against O*(sqrt(nT)) full information. Cited by Bubeck et al. 2012 as the d sqrt(n) lower bound for the hypercube. PDF text not readable here, so the exact theorem and constant are unverified.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization (Shamir)
papers.claim: Theorem 6: on W = [-1,1]^d, regret >= c(d-1)sqrt(T) for T >= d^4/4, with stochastic losses whose mean is in the l1 ball and whose tails are sub-Gaussian (not almost-surely bounded). States it matches the O(d sqrt T) upper bound.

triage.summary: No log-free O(√(dT)) upper bound and no matching Ω(√(dT log T)) lower bound found for adversarial linear bandits on the unit ball with ℓ2-ball losses. The best upper bound is still 3√(dT log T) (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade 2012). Jacobsen, Baudry, Ito & Cesa-Bianchi (2026) call the minimax rate the 'folklore' Θ̃(√(dT)), with logs hidden. Their adversarial lower bound only has the weaker √(dT)·√(d/max(d, log T)) form (and covers direction regret). Their conjecture for the unconstrained problem, which they leave open, would suggest √(dT) for unit-ball comparators. Lévy et al. (COLT 2026) get O(d√(T log T)) on the ball, which doesn't improve things. No source explicitly calls the log gap open. Tool failures: the banditalgs.com post (expired certificate), archive.org (blocked) and the Lattimore–Szepesvári book PDF (unreadable binary) could not be checked.

papers.title: A Perturbation Approach to Unconstrained Linear Bandits (Jacobsen, Baudry, Ito, Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Calls the unit-ball minimax rate the folklore Θ̃(√(dT)). Theorem 5.2 gives a log-free stochastic lower bound √(dT)/64 ∧ T/(12d), but the adversarial lower bound is only C(√(dT) ∧ T/d)·√(d/(d∨log T)). Conjecture 5.3 on the unconstrained rate is left as an open problem.

papers.title: Self-Concordant Perturbations for Linear Bandits (Lévy, Valeau, Akhavan, Rebeschini)
papers.claim: FTPL gets O(d√(n ln n)) on the ℓ2 ball, matching SCRiBLe; no improvement on the ball.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization (Shamir)
papers.claim: Writes the unit-ball upper bound as O(√(dT)) and calls it brittle; shows Ω(d√T) for balls bounded away from the origin.

triage.summary: I count the √(log K) gap as closed, by a direct consequence of a published result rather than a theorem stated for this setting. The database's upper bound √(2 K M T log K) comes from running EXP3 separately in each context. Audibert & Bubeck (COLT 2009 / JMLR 2010) give INF, which removes the log K factor and gets O(√(nK)) minimax regret in the adversarial K-armed bandit. Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, JMLR 2021) also matches the minimax bound within constants. Running INF or Tsallis-INF per context and applying Cauchy–Schwarz (∑_c √T_c ≤ √(M T)) gives O(√(K M T)), which matches the Ω(√(KT)) lower bound in K and T. A standard block construction would also give Ω(√(K M T)) in M, but that is my own derivation: I didn't find it stated in a paper or in the sources I read. Caveats: INF's guarantee is for pseudo-regret / expected regret against an oblivious adversary, so check that this matches the database's regret notion. I took the Audibert–Bubeck claim from search-result summaries and did not fetch the full text, so the theorem number and constant are unchecked. I also didn't look for an explicit statement of the contextual √(KMT) bound, for example in Lattimore–Szepesvári's contextual-bandits chapter.

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Adversarial and Stochastic Bandits
papers.claim: Audibert & Bubeck (COLT 2009; JMLR 2010 version 'Regret Bounds and Minimax Policies under Partial Monitoring'). INF (Implicitly Normalized Forecaster) gets O(√(nK)) regret in adversarial K-armed bandits, removing EXP3's log K factor. Applied per context, this gives O(√(K M T)) for finitely many adversarial contexts.

papers.title: Tsallis-INF: An Optimal Algorithm for Stochastic and Adversarial Bandits
papers.claim: Zimmert & Seldin. Online mirror descent with 1/2-Tsallis entropy gets pseudo-regret in the adversarial regime that is optimal within constants (order √(KT), no log K). Running it per context gives O(√(K M T)).

triage.summary: Closed in the worst-case-over-instances sense. Theorem 8 of Bubeck, Perchet and Rigollet (COLT 2013, arXiv:1302.1611), read from a text version of the arXiv PDF fetched through the r.jina.ai proxy, covers two arms, unit-variance Gaussians and a learner that knows only mu*. Instances: nu0 = N(0,1) x N(-1,1) and nu_Delta = N(-Delta,1) x N(0,1) for Delta in (0,1], so mu* = 0 throughout. Statement: for any policy and any n, max(R_n(nu0), sup_Delta Delta*R_n(nu_Delta)) >= (1/2) log(n/139). The paper reads this as 'regret of order log(n)/Delta is unavoidable for some Delta when only mu* is known'. My own step, not stated in the paper: since R_n(nu_Delta) <= n*Delta, the Delta attaining the sup has n*Delta^2 >~ log n, so log n ~ log(1/Delta). Hence no uniform guarantee of order C/Delta, or o(log(1/Delta))/Delta, is possible, and the log(1/Delta)/Delta upper bound (Garivier, Menard and Stoltz 2019, Theorem C.1, taken from the database; I could not read that PDF) is order-optimal in Delta. A per-instance log(1/Delta)/Delta lower bound cannot hold, because an algorithm tuned to one Delta gets order 1/Delta there, so the per-instance 1/(4 Delta) from Theorem 5 (where Delta is also known) remains correct. The K 'poly_gap' is a bookkeeping artefact since K = 2 is fixed. Several fetches failed: the raw arXiv PDFs of 1302.1611 (v1, v2) and 1602.07182 and the PMLR PDF would not extract, and sbubeck.com refused the connection. The r.jina.ai text version of 1302.1611 worked.

papers.title: Bounded regret in stochastic multi-armed bandits
papers.claim: Theorem 8: two-armed unit-variance Gaussians with only mu* known (nu0 = N(0,1) x N(-1,1), nu_Delta = N(-Delta,1) x N(0,1)). For any policy and any n, max(R_n(nu0), sup_{Delta in (0,1]} Delta*R_n(nu_Delta)) >= (1/2) log(n/139), so regret of order log(n)/Delta, and hence log(1/Delta)/Delta, is unavoidable for some Delta. Theorem 5, where both mu* and Delta are known, gives the 1/Delta-order lower bound.

papers.title: Explore First, Exploit Next: The True Shape of Regret in Bandit Problems
papers.claim: Source of the database's upper bound (Theorem C.1): sum_i (3*Delta_i + 36 log(17/Delta_i)/Delta_i) with mu* known. Not verified in this session because the PDF could not be read.

triage.summary: The gap is closed. Huang, Dai and Huang (ICML 2022, arXiv 2201.11921) study rewards whose α-th moment is bounded by σ^α. In this database's notation, α = 1+eps_m and σ is the moment bound. Their algorithm HTINF assumes α and σ are known. I read their Theorem A.1 on ar5iv: it gives worst-case regret R_T ≤ 30·σ·K^{1−1/α}·(T+1)^{1/α}, with no log factor, in both stochastic and adversarial environments. That equals O(K^{eps/(1+eps)} T^{1/(1+eps)}). It matches the Ω(K^{eps/(1+eps)} T^{1/(1+eps)}) lower bound of Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (2013, Theorem 2) up to constants in both K and T, and the paper says so itself. The same paper's AdaTINF reaches the same order without knowing α or σ, but I only saw that in the abstract. So the extra sqrt-log(K) factor in the database's upper bound (from tajdini2025improved) is not needed. Separately, the database's upper-bound expression, sqrt(K)·T^{1/(1+eps)}·log(K)^{eps/(1+eps)}, has a K exponent of 1/2 rather than eps/(1+eps). The two agree only at eps=1, so that entry is worth checking. Lee, Yang, Lim and Oh (NeurIPS 2020, APE2) and Lee and Lim (minimax-optimal heavy-tailed bandits, IEEE TNNLS 2024) also claim minimax optimality. I could not check their exact bounds (fetching the NeurIPS PDF failed), so the verdict rests on Huang et al. 2022.

papers.title: Adaptive Best-of-Both-Worlds Algorithm for Heavy-Tailed Multi-Armed Bandits (Jiatai Huang, Yan Dai, Longbo Huang; ICML 2022)
papers.claim: HTINF, with known α (=1+eps) and σ, has worst-case regret ≤ 30σK^{1-1/α}(T+1)^{1/α} with no log factor, in stochastic or adversarial environments (Theorem 4.1 / A.1). This matches the Bubeck et al. 2013 lower bound Ω(σK^{1-1/α}T^{1/α}). AdaTINF reaches the same order without knowing α or σ.

papers.title: Bandits with heavy tail (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Lugosi)
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(K^{eps/(1+eps)} T^{1/(1+eps)}), which holds even when eps and the moment bound are known (cited by Huang et al. 2022).

triage.summary:
For K-armed stochastic bandits with a fixed, known, strongly observable feedback graph, the literature already pins down the instance-dependent rate. It is c*(θ, G)·log T, where c* is the value of a linear program built from the graph and the instance (roughly, a minimum-cost exploration budget over the arms). Neither of your database's bounds reflects this. The upper bounds come from plain bandit algorithms that ignore the graph (UCB1, KL-UCB). The lower bound is just Ω(log T). So the polynomial gaps you see in Δ and K are an artefact of the incomplete database, not an open problem.

- **Lower bound.** Buccapatnam, Eryilmaz and Shroff proved an asymptotic Lai–Robbins-style lower bound that depends on the network structure. Their UCB-type and randomized policies match it up to a factor that does not depend on the network.
- **Matching upper bounds.** Wu, György and Szepesvári (NeurIPS 2015) proved problem-dependent lower bounds that do not need T → ∞. Their algorithms match those bounds up to a universal constant. A slide deck (ICML 2022) says their result is exactly asymptotically optimal in the {σ, ∞} case, which is the graph-feedback case. Marinov, Mohri and Zimmert (NeurIPS 2022) give an algorithm that is quasi-optimal both in finite time and asymptotically. They also show that no algorithm can reach the asymptotic constant c* in finite time on some instances.
- **Still open (refinements, not the main gap).** Marinov et al. leave open which graphs allow the finite-time rate to match the asymptotic rate up to constants. They also leave open graphs that change over time and the case where the learner does not know the graph.

Caveat: these results are stated for Gaussian or sub-Gaussian-type rewards. I did not check whether anyone has proved an exactly matching asymptotic constant for general [0,1] rewards (a KL- or Kinf-based constant). The order c*(G, Δ)·log T is settled up to constant factors.

papers.title: Stochastic Online Learning with Feedback Graphs: Finite-Time and Asymptotic Optimality
papers.claim: Marinov, Mohri, Zimmert (NeurIPS 2022). For a fixed, known feedback graph, gives an algorithm that is quasi-optimal both in finite time and asymptotically relative to the LP-based constant c*. Shows that no algorithm can reach c* in finite time on some instances, and gives a family of graphs where it can be reached.

papers.title: Online Learning with Gaussian Payoffs and Side Observations
papers.claim: Wu, György, Szepesvári (NeurIPS 2015). Proves problem-dependent lower bounds that do not need T → ∞, and gives algorithms matching them up to a universal constant (and the minimax bounds up to log factors). A later slide deck says the result is asymptotically optimal in the {σ, ∞} (graph-feedback) case.

papers.title: Reward Maximization Under Uncertainty: Leveraging Side-Observations on Networks
papers.claim: Buccapatnam, Eryilmaz, Shroff. Asymptotic lower bound for uniformly good policies that depends on the network structure. UCB-type and randomized policies match it up to a factor independent of the network.

triage.summary: The setting is from Cesa-Bianchi, Cesari, Colomboni, Fusco, Leonardi (STOC 2024, arXiv 2307.09478): repeated first-price auctions with unknown valuations, full feedback, stochastic i.i.d. environment. Theorem 4 gives an O(sqrt(T ln T)) upper bound; it is stated for transparent feedback, which also covers full feedback. Theorem 5 gives a sqrt(T)/2048 lower bound. The authors describe the rate as Theta~(sqrt T), tight up to poly-log factors. In the first 100k of about 177k characters of the paper (the conclusion was not read), they do not call the log gap an open problem. Their remark about shaving off a log term refers to the transparent-feedback analysis (Exp3.FPA). Related work found carries extra log factors or does not apply: Han-Zhou-Weissman 2003.09795 (sqrt(T)·log^2 T in Theorem 1, O(sqrt T log^2.5 T) in a later abstract, for i.i.d. values); Han et al. 2007.04568 (chaining, Õ(sqrt T), adversarial setting with Lipschitz policies); Achddou et al. ACML 2021 (log^2 T regret only when the distribution of competitors' highest bid is known, T^{1/3+eps} when it must be learned). No log-free sqrt(T) upper bound was found, and no explicit open-problem statement was found.

papers.title: The Role of Transparency in Repeated First-Price Auctions with Unknown Valuations
papers.claim: Full/transparent feedback, stochastic i.i.d.: O(sqrt(T ln T)) upper bound (Thm 4) and Omega(sqrt T) lower bound (Thm 5); rate Theta~(sqrt T), tight up to poly-log factors.

papers.title: Optimal No-regret Learning in Repeated First-price Auctions
papers.claim: Õ(sqrt T) regret for i.i.d. private values from an unknown distribution (sqrt(T)·log^2 T in Theorem 1, O(sqrt T log^2.5 T) in a later abstract); notes that the Omega(sqrt T) lower bound is standard even with full information.

papers.title: Learning to Bid Optimally and Efficiently in Adversarial First-price Auctions
papers.claim: Hierarchical expert chaining gives minimax-optimal Õ(sqrt T) regret against Lipschitz bidding policies in the adversarial setting; still has log factors.

triage.summary: Li, Wang and Zhou (COLT 2019) close this gap up to iterated-logarithm factors. The setting is finite-armed linear contextual bandits with K arms per round and adversarially chosen (oblivious) action sets. Their lower bound is Ω(√(dT log T log K)), proved for K ≤ 2^{d/2} under a horizon condition. Their VCL-SupLinUCB algorithm has an upper bound of O(√(dT log T log K))·poly(log log(KT)). This is two √log T factors better than SupLinUCB's bound of √(dT log^3(KT)), the upper bound in our database. The lower bound is also stronger than the database's √(dT) lower bound. The only remaining gap is a poly(log log) factor. The database's per-variable T-exponent gap (log^1.5 against 0.5) should be updated to: upper √(T log T)·polyloglog, lower √(T log T). One caveat: the lower bound needs K ≤ 2^{d/2}. A related recent paper, Jin (arXiv 2609.15170), studies action sets chosen adaptively, which is a different setting from the oblivious sequence here. Its bounds include a K^{1/4} factor, so it does not apply.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Yingkai Li, Yining Wang, Yuan Zhou)
papers.claim: For finite-armed linear contextual bandits with adversarial action sets and n ≤ 2^{d/2} arms: lower bound Ω(√(dT log T log n)); VCL-SupLinUCB upper bound poly(log log(nT))·O(√(dT log T log n)). This matches up to iterated-log factors and saves two √log T factors over SupLinUCB.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linear Contextual Bandits with Arbitrary Adaptive Action Sets (Tianyuan Jin)
papers.claim: In a setting where action sets are chosen adaptively, with K ≤ d: matching bounds of order K^{1/4}√(dT) up to logs. With K ≥ d: bounds of order √(dT)·min{√d, (d log K)^{1/4}}. This is a different setting from the oblivious action sets here.

triage.summary:
This setting comes from Dai, Xu, Qi and Jordan, "Incentive-Aware Recommender Systems in Two-Sided Markets" (arXiv:2211.15381). The log T gap in the database is caused by setting δ=1/T. It is not a real open problem.

What the paper states (read from the arXiv HTML version):
- **Upper bound (Theorem 5.2).** With η=√(8 ln m/T), the MARP policy satisfies R_T ≤ √((T/2) ln m) + √((T/2) ln(1/δ)) with probability at least 1−δ.
- **Lower bound (Theorem 5.3).** The minimax regret satisfies lim_{m→∞} lim_{T→∞} R†_T / ((1−ε_T)√(T ln m/2)) = 1.
- **Optimality claim.** The authors say MARP is minimax optimal.

Why the gap disappears:
- **Fixed δ.** For any constant confidence level, the upper bound is Θ(√(T log m)), which matches the lower bound's rate in both T and m. The leading constants also match asymptotically: √(T ln m/2) on both sides.
- **Expected regret.** I did this calculation myself; the paper does not state it. The high-probability bound has a sub-Gaussian tail, so integrating it gives E[R_T] ≤ √((T/2) ln m) + √(πT/8). That is O(√(T log m)) with no log T factor, so it matches the lower bound in T. The extra term is order √T and does not grow with m, so the leading constant still matches as m→∞.
- **Where the log T comes from.** Only plugging in δ=1/T adds a √(T log T) term, which is where the database's log_gap comes from.

Caveats:
- The lower bound is asymptotic (m→∞ after T→∞), so the paper does not show the constants match for a fixed m.
- The Hedge-type √(T log m) rate is unusual for bandit feedback, where the standard lower bound is √(KT). It must rely on the specific incentive/opportunity-cost structure of this model. I did not check that part of the paper; my fetch covered only the first ~100k of ~170k characters.
- I found no other paper on this exact setting.

Bottom line: for fixed δ, and for expected regret, the rates in T and K match, and the paper itself claims minimax optimality.

papers.title: Incentive-Aware Recommender Systems in Two-Sided Markets
papers.claim: Theorem 5.2: with probability at least 1−δ, R_T ≤ √((T/2) ln m) + √((T/2) ln(1/δ)). Theorem 5.3: the minimax regret is asymptotically (1−ε_T)√(T ln m/2) as m→∞ after T→∞. The authors say MARP achieves the minimax regret, so for fixed δ (or in expectation, by integrating the tail) there is no log T gap.

triage.summary: The database's best upper bound (Dani et al. 2008, d√T·log^1.5 T) is not the state of the art. OFUL (Abbasi-Yadkori et al. 2011) gets O(d√T log T); I saw this cited by 1904.00242 and 2502.17175, not in the paper itself. Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (2012) get order d√(T log T) for any compact action set. Their result is adversarial but applies here because rewards are bounded. They say that without further assumptions it is minimax optimal 'up to a logarithmic factor'; I saw this in a search snippet, not the paper. The lower bound is still Ω(d√T) (Dani et al. 2008; Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis 2010 for the unit ball). Li, Wang & Zhou (2019) prove Ω(d√(T log T)), but only for infinite action sets that change over time, so it does not cover a fixed compact set. For ellipsoids, arXiv 2502.17175 gets d√T with no log factor, but makes no claim for general compact sets. So a √(log T) gap remains for fixed arbitrary compact sets. The literature describes the rate as known only up to log factors (e.g. Θ̃(d√T) in 2608.14319), but I found no explicit statement that removing the last √(log T) is an open problem. A fixed-set d√(T log T) lower bound could exist that my searches missed. I did not check the Lattimore–Szepesvári book directly. Recommendation: raise the upper bound to d√(T log T); the remaining gap is √(log T) in T and none in d.

papers.title: Towards minimax policies for online linear optimization with bandit feedback (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Kakade)
papers.claim: Regret of order d√(n log n) for any compact action set (adversarial, so it also covers the bounded stochastic case). The authors say it is minimax optimal up to a logarithmic factor without further assumptions on the action set. Seen in a search snippet, not the paper itself.

papers.title: Improved Algorithms for Linear Stochastic Bandits (Abbasi-Yadkori, Pál, Szepesvári)
papers.claim: OFUL achieves O(d√T log T) regret, as cited by 1904.00242 and 2502.17175; not checked in the paper itself.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Li, Wang, Zhou)
papers.claim: Ω(d√(T log T)) lower bound, but only when the infinite action set changes over time. The standard fixed-action-set lower bound is Ω(d√T).

papers.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms
papers.claim: E2TC achieves order dσ√T with no log factor for ellipsoid action sets, matching the lower bound there. No claim for arbitrary compact sets.

papers.title: Quantum Multi-Armed Bandits and Linear Bandits: Lower Bounds and Algorithms (Liu, Li, Lui)
papers.claim: Describes the classical general-action-set rate as Θ̃(d√T), i.e. known only up to log factors (upper O(d√T log T), lower Ω(d√T)).

triage.summary: The gap between d√(T log T) (Russo-Van Roy, Dong-Van Roy) and d√T (Dani et al.) is closed only under a stronger noise assumption. Gouverneur et al. (arXiv:2403.03361) prove Bayesian regret ≤ 7d√T for Two-Step Thompson Sampling (2-TS) on any compact action set inside the unit ball, convex or not. However, they need a 'smooth rewards' condition: R_a − R_b must be ρ(a,b)-sub-Gaussian, plus separability. Generic bounded ±1 noise that is independent across actions does not satisfy this, so the result does not cover this setting as stated. The follow-up arXiv:2502.02140 still has d√(T log T). On the lower-bound side, Li-Wang-Zhou (COLT 2019) prove Ω(√(dT log T log n)) only for action sets that change every round (contextual), which does not transfer to a fixed action set. No source I saw states the fixed-action-set, bounded-noise case as an explicit open problem, hence 'blank'. The gap looks closed in spirit, but only under an extra assumption.

papers.title: Chained Information-Theoretic Bounds and Tight Regret Rate for Linear Bandit Problems
papers.claim: Two-Step Thompson Sampling (2-TS) achieves Bayesian regret ≤ 7 d sqrt(T) for compact action sets in the unit ball, under a smooth-rewards assumption (sub-Gaussian increments w.r.t. Euclidean metric, plus separability); removes the log T factor under that assumption.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis for Thompson Sampling with Many Actions
papers.claim: Rate-distortion analysis gives O(d sqrt(T log T)) Bayesian regret for TS in d-dim linear bandits with infinite action sets.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Thompson Sampling with Infinite Action Spaces
papers.claim: Recovers the O(d sqrt(T log T)) rate with improved constants for infinite/continuous action spaces.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits
papers.claim: Lower bound Omega(sqrt(dT log T log n)) for linear contextual bandits with n <= 2^{d/2} actions per round (time-varying action sets), showing the log T factor is necessary in the contextual setting.

triage.summary: He, Zhou, Zhang & Gu (NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2205.06811) close the polynomial gap in T and d up to log factors. I read their arXiv HTML v2 (first 100k of 121k characters). Their setting matches ours on the main points. The adversary is adaptive and corrupts after seeing the decision set, the chosen action and the stochastic reward. The budget C = Σ|c_k| is per-path. A new, arbitrary decision set arrives each round and may be infinite, with ‖x‖₂ ≤ L. Noise is conditionally R-sub-Gaussian. I did not confirm from the text that regret is measured against uncorrupted rewards; that is the standard convention. CW-OFUL achieves Õ(d√T + dC) when C is known (Theorem 4.2). When C is unknown, it gets Õ(d√T + dC̄) for C ≤ C̄ (Theorem 4.9). The paper proves matching lower bounds Ω(max{d√T, dC}) (Propositions 4.7 and 4.8). This improves our upper bound (ding2021robust, which scales as T^{3/4}√d(C+1)) to the rate T^{1/2} and d^1, matching our Ω(d√(T log T)) lower bound up to log factors. Only log-factor gaps remain. The bound has no K dependence, so it is consistent with the K^{1/4} lower bound. I did not search for a corruption-robust SupLinUCB-type √(dT log K) bound, so the exact dependence on K for small K is not settled by this search. I ran one search; the PDF fetch returned unreadable binary, and the HTML fetch worked.

papers.title: Nearly Optimal Algorithms for Linear Contextual Bandits with Adversarial Corruptions
papers.claim: Linear contextual bandits with adaptive adversarial corruption (total budget C on chosen actions), arbitrary time-varying decision sets, and conditionally R-sub-Gaussian noise. CW-OFUL achieves Õ(d√T + dC) regret for known C (Thm 4.2) and Õ(d√T + dC̄) for unknown C when C ≤ C̄ (Thm 4.9). Lower bound Ω(max{d√T, dC}) (Props 4.7 and 4.8). Ω(T) regret is unavoidable for unknown large C (Thm 4.12).

triage.summary: The database bounds come from Falahatgar et al. (ICML 2017). Its ranking upper bound is O(K log K (log log K)^3 / eps^2) at delta = 1/K, and its lower bound is Omega(K log(K/delta)/eps^2). A follow-up by the same group, 'The Limits of Maxing, Ranking, and Preference Learning' (Falahatgar, Jain, Orlitsky, Pichapati, Ravindrakumar, ICML 2018), says in its abstract that under SST and STI it derives a ranking algorithm with 'optimal O(n log n) complexity'. That claim removes the (log log n)^3 factor. Pichapati's UCSD thesis (eScholarship) appears to make the same claim, but that page returned HTTP 429, so I only saw it via a search snippet. Caveat: I read only the abstract (PMLR and ICML pages). PDF text extraction failed, so I did not see the exact eps/delta dependence or the theorem number. The intended bound is presumably O(K log K / eps^2) for delta = 1/K, which would match the lower bound. Ren-Liu-Shroff (arXiv:1806.02970) gives tight PAC total-ranking bounds, but only under the MNL/Plackett-Luce model, not the general SST+STI class.

papers.title: The Limits of Maxing, Ranking, and Preference Learning (Falahatgar, Jain, Orlitsky, Pichapati, Ravindrakumar)
papers.claim: Under Strong Stochastic Transitivity and Stochastic Triangle Inequality, gives a PAC ranking algorithm with 'optimal O(n log n)' comparison complexity (abstract). This removes the (log log n)^3 factor of the 2017 bound. The eps/delta dependence was not verified.

papers.title: Maximum Selection and Ranking under Noisy Comparisons (Falahatgar, Orlitsky, Pichapati, Suresh)
papers.claim: Ranking with O(n log n (log log n)^3 / eps^2) comparisons for delta = 1/n, optimal up to a (log log n)^3 factor. These are the database's current bounds.

papers.title: PAC Ranking from Pairwise and Listwise Queries: Lower Bounds and Upper Bounds (Ren, Liu, Shroff)
papers.claim: Tight lower and upper bounds for PAC total ranking, but only under the MNL/Plackett-Luce model (a special case).

triage.summary:
The polynomial gap is closed, but only because the database is missing two known results. The database pairs a gap-free upper bound, O(√(KT)), with the weaker lower bound min(K/Δ, ΔT).

(1) Upper bound. MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck) achieves O(min{√(KT), (K/Δ)·log(TΔ²/K)}), where Δ is the smallest gap. I saw this bound credited to MOSS in the survey by Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi (arXiv 1204.5721). It does not even need to know Δ. In the regime Δ ≥ √(K/T) this gives K/Δ up to a log factor, so the exponents become Δ: −1, K: 1, T: 0 (polylog only).

(2) Lower bound. Theorem 11 of Lattimore's 'Regret Analysis of the Anytime Optimally Confident UCB Algorithm' (arXiv 1603.08661) is a finite-time bound that holds for any strategy. For every instance μ, either the regret on μ is at least (1/4)Σ_i (1/Δ_i) log(nΔ_i²/(k_i log n)), or there is a perturbed instance μ' where one arm's mean is raised by 2Δ_i that suffers at least half the analogous sum. Here k_i = Σ_j min{1, Δ_i/Δ_j}, which equals K when all gaps are equal. If every gap is Δ, both μ and μ' have gaps of at least Δ. Because the theorem covers every strategy, including ones that know Δ, it gives a worst-case lower bound over this class of Ω((K/Δ)·log(TΔ²/(K log T))). Specialising the theorem to equal gaps is my own step; the paper states only the instance-dependent form. Separately, gaps of about √(K/T) are allowed whenever Δ ≤ √(K/T), which gives the standard Ω(√(KT)).

So the worst-case regret is Θ(min{√(KT), (K/Δ)·log(TΔ²/K)}), up to at most a log-log factor inside the log term. In particular, the ΔT branch of the database's lower bound is not the binding term at the minimax level.

Caveats:
- Lattimore's lower bound is proved for unit-variance Gaussian noise, not rewards in [0,1]. The usual Bernoulli adaptation (means in [1/4, 3/4]) should give the same rate, but I did not see that version stated.
- I could not read the PDF of Lattimore's JMLR 2018 paper 'Refining the Confidence Level for Optimistic Bandit Strategies'. Its abstract says it contains a nearly matching finite-time lower bound.
- I did not fetch the original MOSS paper, so the MOSS bound comes from the survey's attribution.
- Bubeck, Perchet & Rigollet (COLT 2013, arXiv 1302.1611) say in their abstract that bounded regret is impossible when only Δ is known, which agrees with a T-dependent (log) lower bound. A Microsoft Research page flags their Theorem 8 as having an incorrect proof; I did not check which result that theorem is.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of the Anytime Optimally Confident UCB Algorithm
papers.claim: Theorem 11 (Gaussian noise): for any strategy, either the regret on μ is at least (1/4)Σ_i (1/Δ_i) log(nΔ_i²/(k_i log n)), or an instance μ' with one gap raised to 2Δ_i has regret at least half the analogous sum. With all gaps equal to Δ (k_i = K), this gives a worst-case lower bound of Ω((K/Δ) log(nΔ²/(K log n))) over instances with gaps of at least Δ. This specialisation is our inference; the paper states only the instance-dependent form.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems
papers.claim: Survey by Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi. It credits MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck) with regret O(min{√(nK), (K/Δ) ln(nΔ²/K)}), where Δ is the smallest gap.

papers.title: Bounded regret in stochastic multi-armed bandits
papers.claim: Bubeck, Perchet & Rigollet. The abstract says their lower bounds show bounded regret is impossible when only the gap lower bound Δ is known, and that bounded regret is achievable when both μ* and Δ are known.

papers.title: Refining the Confidence Level for Optimistic Bandit Strategies
papers.claim: Lattimore, JMLR 19. Its abstract says it gives a finite-time lower bound that very nearly matches the finite-time upper bound of a strategy that is both minimax optimal and asymptotically optimal. The theorem itself was not read: PDF extraction failed.

triage.summary:
Under the usual stochastic linear bandit model (reward ⟨a,θ⟩ plus independent noise, unit-ball actions, θ in the unit l2 ball), the minimax rate is Θ(d√T) with no log T factor. This means the database entry has two problems.

1. **The lower bound is too weak.** Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis (2010) and Lattimore & Szepesvári (Bandit Algorithms, Thm 24.2) prove Ω(d√T) on the unit ball. The second-hand search excerpts and the Zhang et al. paper both report this; I did not open those two sources myself. This is stronger than the √(dT) bounds recorded.

2. **The upper bound is probably wrongly inherited.** The 3√(dT log T) bound comes from the adversarial bandit linear optimisation results (Bubeck–Cesa-Bianchi–Kakade 2012; Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi 2012 survey). Those assume the observed loss is exactly ⟨a, z_t⟩. With additive noise the observation is not linear in a, so the reduction fails. If it held, it would contradict the Ω(d√T) lower bound.

**Matching bounds.** Zhang, Hadiji & Combes (arXiv:2502.17175, 2025), which I fetched, gives both sides on ellipsoids, which include the unit ball:
- **Lower bound (Thm 2.1):** regret ≥ min(σd√T/16, BT/4) for any parameter norm B.
- **Upper bound (Thm 3.1, E2TC algorithm):** regret ≤ 6dσ√T + lower-order terms, giving O(min(σd√T + d‖θ‖, T‖θ‖)) (Cor. 3.1).
- **Applied here:** with ‖θ‖ ≤ 1, bounded ±1 noise is 1-sub-Gaussian, so the upper bound is O(d√T). Their lower bound uses Gaussian noise. I expect the same construction to give Ω(d√T) for bounded noise (e.g. Rademacher/Bernoulli rewards), but I have not checked that.

**Caveat.** If the database instead means the iid-loss-vector model (observe ⟨a, z_t⟩ with z_t iid in the unit ball, a special case of the adversarial model), then the √(dT log T) vs √(dT) gap is a different question, and I found no source closing it in this session. The 'bounded_pm1' noise label points to the additive-noise model, so the verdict is closed at Θ(d√T). The database should fix both the upper bound (drop the adversarial inheritance) and the lower bound (raise it to d√T).

papers.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms (Raymond Zhang, Hedi Hadiji, Richard Combes)
papers.claim: Ellipsoid action sets (unit ball included), sub-Gaussian noise with variance proxy σ². Thm 2.1: any algorithm has regret ≥ min(σd√T/16, BT/4). triage.summary:
I found no published result that closes this gap. The only lower bound that would close it was retracted by its own authors, so the question is known to be open.

**The gap.** In the regime T→∞, the upper bound is of order log(1/Δ)/Δ and the lower bound is of order 1/Δ. They differ by a log(1/Δ) factor; the extra K-dependence matters little for K=2.

**The retracted claim.** Bubeck, Perchet & Rigollet (COLT 2013, arXiv:1302.1611) study the case where the learner knows μ* but not Δ. Their abstract says that "bounded regret of order 1/Δ is not possible if one only knows μ*". Their introduction says that logarithmic growth of the rescaled regret ΔR_n is unavoidable even when μ* is known. This is their Theorem 8, which would make the log(1/Δ)/Δ rate tight.

**The erratum.** The paper's Microsoft Research page carries this note, which I fetched and saw directly: "The proof of Theorem 8 is not correct. We do not know if the theorem holds true." The arXiv page (v2, Feb 2013) has no erratum. Garivier, Ménard & Stoltz (2019) cite the erratum and only point to later work showing bounded regret is achievable when μ* is known (Bubeck et al. 2013; Faure et al. 2015).

**What's left.** I found nothing that proves Theorem 8 or improves the upper bound to O(1/Δ) when Δ is unknown. So whether the log(1/Δ) factor is necessary for K=2 Gaussian arms with μ* and σ known is still unresolved. My searches can't rule out a recent paper that fixes it.

**Caveats.** I couldn't read the full Theorem 8 statement, so I'm relying on how the abstract, introduction and erratum describe it. I also couldn't read the appendices of arXiv:1602.07182, so I didn't check whether the database's Theorem A.3 and C.1 come from that paper.

papers.title: Bounded regret in stochastic multi-armed bandits (Bubeck, Perchet, Rigollet), COLT 2013
papers.claim: Studies the case where μ* is known (plus a lower bound on Δ) and gives a policy with bounded regret. Its abstract says bounded regret of order 1/Δ is impossible if only μ* is known, and its introduction says logarithmic growth of ΔR_n is unavoidable even when μ* is known (Theorem 8). The authors' erratum on the Microsoft Research page says: 'The proof of Theorem 8 is not correct. We do not know if the theorem holds true.'

triage.summary: No published result closes the log²(NT) vs log(NT) gap in the gap-dependent term, and the gap is acknowledged but not formally posed as open. The upper bound in the database (hu2025robust Corollary 1) is from Hu, Wang & Chen, arXiv 2511.10344 (AAAI 2026): O(C/V + Σ ln²(VT)/(VΔ_k) + K ln(VT) ln(1/Δ)/(VΔ)). That paper gives no lower bound for the corrupted setting and calls its result "near-optimal." For the Byzantine variant it explicitly calls the remaining ln² vs ln gap "an interesting open question for future work." The earlier Hu & Chen paper (arXiv 2502.07514, NeurIPS 2025) proves a multi-agent bound with log(VT)·log(KVT) per gap (MA-BARBAT, Theorem 2). Its Table 1 compares this with a lower bound of C/V + Σ log T/(VΔ_k), obtained by combining Gupta et al. 2019 with the stochastic lower bound, and it claims optimality only up to a log factor. FTRL/Tsallis-INF methods, which get a single log in the single-agent case, are noted to be hard to extend to the multi-agent setting. No multi-agent FTRL or best-of-both-worlds corrupted result was found. Other multi-agent corruption papers (Ghaffari et al. 2106.04207; 2411.08167) give weaker or differently structured bounds. Labelling this "open_known" is borderline: the gap is acknowledged implicitly ("near-optimal up to log") and stated as open only for the Byzantine version. The final sections of both Hu papers were not read.

triage.summary: The gap is closed by the same paper that gives the database's lower bound: Ito (NeurIPS 2021, arXiv:2109.10963). For the expert (full-information) problem in the adversarial regime with a self-bounding constraint, it proves an upper bound of O(log K/Δ + sqrt(C log K/Δ)). Anytime Hedge with a decreasing learning rate and second-order-bound algorithms achieve it, without needing to know C or Δ. The paper says this is tight up to constants and that Theorem 5 is the matching lower bound. Hedge also has the worst-case bound O(sqrt(T log K)), so the upper bound matches min(sqrt(T log K), sqrt(C log K/Δ) + log K/Δ) up to constants. The database's upper bounds came from bandit algorithms (Tsallis-INF, Masoudian & Seldin), which is why it showed a polynomial gap in K, T and Δ. Ito defines regret on the corrupted losses, which matches regret_reference=corrupted. I read the abstract and introduction, not the proofs.

triage.summary: In the worst-case regime the bounds already match at Theta(sqrt(KT)); the gap is an artifact of the database reading exponents with Delta and C held fixed. Upper bound: Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, JMLR 2021) gives 4*sqrt(KT)+1 at every instance in the self-bounding regime. Lower bound: Ito 2021 (arXiv 2109.10963, Theorem 6) gives Omega(min{sqrt(KT), sqrt(C K/Delta) + K/Delta}) for each fixed (C, Delta). Taking the supremum over instances with C=0 (the stochastic case, which the regime includes) and Delta ~ sqrt(K/T) gives K/Delta = sqrt(KT), so the minimum is sqrt(KT). The classical stochastic minimax lower bound (Auer et al. 2002) would give the same, but I am citing it from standard knowledge; it did not appear in this session's searches. Knowing C and Delta does not help the learner in the worst case. Verification limits: searches confirmed the title of 2109.10963 and that it gives nearly tight lower bounds in this regime, but the snippet seen was the expert-problem version, Omega(min{log N/Delta + sqrt(C log N/Delta), sqrt(T log N)}); the bandit Theorem 6 form is taken from the database entry, and the author name Shinji Ito is from memory. Only the instance-dependent log-factor gap (log T vs log(T/C) in the corruption term) remains open; it does not affect the worst-case regime.

triage.summary: The gap is closed: worst-case regret for adversarial K-armed bandits with decoupled feedback is Θ(√(KT)). Avner, Mannor & Shamir (ICML 2012), footnote 1 of Section 3, say the standard Ω(√(KT)) bandit lower bound carries over to decoupled algorithms. Their reason is that the difficulty comes from distinguishing slightly different distributions from T observations, which decoupling does not change. This is a remark with justification, not a formal theorem. Their Theorem 6 gives a formal c√(kT) lower bound only for decoupled algorithms whose exploration distribution is fixed. On the upper side, Rouyer & Seldin (COLT 2020) prove O(√(KT)) for Decoupled-Tsallis-INF and call it minimax optimal; jin2023improved matches this rate. The database's √(T log K) lower bound is simply weaker than the known Ω(√(KT)) bound. Exponents: K^{1/2}, T^{1/2}.

triage.summary:
I read "worst_case" in the usual way: the minimax regret, taken over all allowed structure classes and all instances in them. Under that reading the gap is already closed at Θ(√T), using standard results.

**Why it is closed:**
- **Lower bound.** One valid structure is the trivial one: every pair of means is allowed. That is the ordinary two-armed Gaussian bandit with known σ. The standard minimax lower bound for that problem (Auer et al. 2002; Lattimore–Szepesvári Ch. 15) is Ω(√((K−1)T)). A survey quotes it as √((K−1)T)/27 for unit-variance Gaussian bandits with means in [0,1]^K; with K=2 this is Ω(√T). The database's best lower bound, log(T/139)/2 from Bubeck–Perchet–Rigollet 2013, is far weaker in the worst case. It is really a lower bound for a specific class, which explains the apparent poly gap.
- **Upper bound.** Any algorithm for unstructured bandits works whatever the structure is. MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck 2009) gets O(√(KT)) minimax regret, which is O(√T) for K=2. This drops the √(log T) factor from the 8√2·√(T log T) bound inherited from Brukhim et al. 2025.

Together these give Θ(√T).

**Caveat.** If the database means the minimax rate for one fixed structure class, then the answer depends on the class. It can be anywhere from O(1) (e.g., Bubeck et al. 2013, where the learner knows extra information such as the gap or the optimal mean, giving bounded regret) up to Θ(√T). In that case, comparing a log T lower bound for one class with a √(T log T) upper bound for every class is not a meaningful gap.

**Gaps in what I checked.** I did not fetch the book's chapter or the Brukhim et al. theorem itself; the claims above come from search-result snippets. The book's theorem number is not confirmed: sources call the Gaussian result Theorem 15.1, Theorem 15.2 or Exercise 15.2, and the published edition would settle this. The Auer et al. (2002) attribution for the lower bound also comes from a later paper quoted in a snippet; I did not see that paper directly.

triage.summary:
The polynomial gap in d appears to be closed up to logarithmic factors. Your database's upper bound is d²·ϑ·√(T log(1/δ)) from Lee et al. 2020; its lower bound is √(dT) from Gerchinovitz & Lattimore 2016.

Upper bound: Zimmert & Lattimore (COLT 2022) give a high-probability bound of order d√(T log(T/δ)) on any compact action set, which includes convex bodies. I saw this on the PMLR page and in search summaries of the PDF. It holds even against adaptive adversaries, so it also covers the oblivious case. That improves the exponent of d from 2 to 1. The same paper also gives an efficient algorithm (FTRL with the entropic barrier) with regret O(d²√T log T), which beats Lee et al.'s efficient d^{7/2}√T·polylog(T) bound.

Lower bound: for worst-case convex bodies, an Ω(d√T) lower bound goes back to Dani, Hayes & Kakade (2007). Two pieces of evidence point to this. Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (2012) say in their abstract that d√(n log n) on compact action sets is minimax optimal up to a log factor. A 2025 arXiv paper (2510.24187, "Self-Concordant Perturbations for Linear Bandits") says, according to the search summary, that Dani et al. (2007) proved an Ω(d√n) minimax lower bound for arbitrary convex bodies. This lower bound is for expected regret; with δ held constant it carries over to high-probability regret. So the d-exponents become 1 and 1, and T stays at 1/2.

Caveats: I could not read the Zimmert–Lattimore PDF (the fetch returned compressed binary) or the lower-bound theorem in Dani et al. So I have not checked directly that Dani et al.'s loss normalization matches your 'polar_of_action_set' condition (|⟨a,ℓ⟩| ≤ 1). The δ-dependence in the matching lower bound is also not pinned down. Your database's √(dT log(1/δ)) bound does have the right δ-scaling, but only for the √(dT) rate. If you want an exact δ-tight match, that remains unverified.

Shamir's theorem was read from the ar5iv HTML. Both arXiv/PMLR PDFs were unreadable by the fetch tool.
