triage.summary:
The √log T gap is closed, apart from iterated-logarithm (log log) factors, by the same paper the database already cites for its lower bound. That paper is Li, Wang & Zhou, "Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits" (COLT 2019, arXiv:1904.00242).

**Setting:** linear contextual bandits with finite action sets of n ≤ 2^{d/2} actions per round, chosen adversarially and changing each round.

**What the paper shows:**
- **Lower bound:** minimax regret is Ω(√(dT log T log n)).
- **Upper bound:** their Variable-Confidence-Level SupLinUCB algorithm matches this lower bound up to iterated-logarithm factors, removing two √log T factors from earlier SupLinUCB analyses.
- **Infinite or very large action sets:** a talk abstract by co-author Yuan Zhou says the paper also gives O(d√(T log T))·poly(log log T), matching Ω(d√(T log T)) up to log log factors.

**Why the database shows a gap:** the stored upper bound is the weaker Thompson-sampling bound (Agrawal & Goyal 2013). The tight upper bound from Theorem-level results in Li–Wang–Zhou is missing from the database.

**Caveats:**
- The rates hold only up to poly(log log T) factors, so the gap is closed in T and d except for log log terms.
- I only read the arXiv abstract and search summaries, not the theorem statements. In particular, the abstract does not state the upper bound explicitly; it only says the algorithm matches the lower bound up to iterated logarithms.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Yingkai Li, Yining Wang, Yuan Zhou)
papers.claim: For linear contextual bandits with n ≤ 2^{d/2} actions per period, minimax regret is Ω(√(dT log T log n)); the VCL SupLinUCB algorithm matches this up to iterated-log factors. Per a co-author's talk abstract, for infinite action sets the upper bound is O(d√(T log T))·poly(log log T), matching the Ω(d√(T log T)) lower bound.

triage.summary: The gap seems to come from how the database recorded the upper bound, not from an open problem. Upper bound: in Bai, Jin, Wang & Xiong (arXiv 2102.11494, NeurIPS 2021), Theorem 5 is for *linear* bandit games and gives O~(d^2/ε^2). Setting d=K (one-hot features) gives the K^2/ε^2 bound in the database. The same paper also handles the finite-action bandit game directly. I read these statements on the ar5iv page. Theorem 2 gives O~(AB/ε^2) samples to reach a (gap_ε + ε)-approximate Stackelberg value. Theorem 3 is a matching lower bound: with about AB/ε^2 or fewer samples (times an absolute constant, with A, B ≥ 3), any algorithm has error g+ε with probability ≥ 1/3 on some instance. If K is the number of arms, meaning leader–follower action pairs (K = AB), the bound is Θ~(K/ε^2) and tight. That matches the Ω(K/ε^2) lower bound credited to li2023tight. Caveats: (1) The database setting is only labelled 'other_pure_exploration, K-armed, Bernoulli'. I assume it is the Stackelberg/bandit-game problem from bai2021sample, so the verdict depends on that reading and on K = AB. (2) The paper's model has noisy rewards, possibly sub-Gaussian/bounded. I didn't check that Theorem 3's hard instances are Bernoulli, though bounded-reward lower bounds of this kind usually are. (3) I could not find or confirm the li2023tight paper. (4) If K instead means each player's action count (A = B = K), the bound is Θ~(K^2/ε^2) by Theorems 2 and 3, which is also tight. Either way, the gap is closed by Theorems 2 and 3 of the same paper.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Learning of Stackelberg Equilibria in General-Sum Games
papers.claim: Theorem 2: bandit games with A leader and B follower actions; O~(AB/ε^2) samples are enough for a (gap_ε+ε)-approximate Stackelberg value. Theorem 3: matching lower bound, Ω(AB/ε^2) samples are needed (A, B ≥ 3). Theorem 5: linear bandit games, O~(d^2/ε^2), which is the source of the database's K^2/ε^2 bound with d=K.

triage.summary: Closed: the minimax regret is Theta(d sqrt(T)) with no log factor. Upper bound: Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (COLT 2012, arXiv:1202.3079). Their abstract says OSMD on the hypercube is efficient and gets d sqrt(n) regret, which beats the database's d sqrt(T log T) by sqrt(log T). I couldn't read the PDF, so I'm assuming the theorem's loss set is the polar of the cube (l1 ball, |<a,l>|<=1). Lévy et al. 2025 (arXiv:2510.24187) also credits O(d sqrt n) on the hypercube to Bubeck et al. 2012. Lower bound: Shamir (COLT 2015, arXiv:1408.2368), Theorem 6: for W=[-1,1]^d, d>1, T>=d^4/4, regret >= c(d-1)sqrt(T), stated as tight up to constants. Caveat: Shamir's losses are stochastic sub-Gaussian with mean in the dual-norm (l1) ball, not bounded in [-1,1] exactly; a bounded version should follow by standard arguments but I didn't verify it. Dani, Hayes & Kakade (NeurIPS 2007) are also credited by secondary sources with an Omega(d sqrt T) lower bound; their abstract only says bandit feedback costs at least a sqrt(n) factor, and I couldn't read their theorems. The database's lower bounds (sqrt(dT), from the multi-armed bandit/simplex case) are loose by a sqrt(d) factor for the hypercube.

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Kakade)
papers.claim: Online Stochastic Mirror Descent on the hypercube is computationally efficient and gets d sqrt(n) regret, with no log factor.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization (Shamir)
papers.claim: Theorem 6: for W=[-1,1]^d, d>1, T>=d^4/4, there is a loss distribution (mean in the dual-norm ball) under which any player has expected regret >= c(d-1)sqrt(T); stated as tight up to constants against an O(d sqrt T) algorithm.

papers.title: The Price of Bandit Information for Online Optimization (Dani, Hayes, Kakade)
papers.claim: Abstract: lower bounds show bandit feedback costs at least a sqrt(n) factor over full information. Secondary sources (Princeton blog; Lévy et al. 2025) credit it with an Omega(d sqrt T) bandit lower bound; I couldn't read its theorems.

papers.title: Self-Concordant Perturbations for Linear Bandits (Lévy et al.)
papers.claim: Credits the Omega(d sqrt n) minimax lower bound to Dani et al. 2007 and the O(d sqrt n) OSMD hypercube upper bound to Bubeck et al. 2012.

triage.summary: The gap is closed up to constants by results missing from the database. Only abstracts and search snippets were checked, not full PDFs. Upper bound: Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, JMLR 2021) gets regret O(sum_i log T/Delta_i + sqrt(C sum_i log T/Delta_i)) in a setting that includes stochastic bandits with adversarial corruption. This is linear in K, has a single log T, matches the Lai-Robbins log T/Delta rate at C=0, and is at most O(sum log T/Delta_i + C) by AM-GM. That removes the extra K and log T factors in the Lykouris et al. 2018 bound. Masoudian & Seldin (COLT 2021) refine the log factor and the C dependence. Lower bound: Ito (NeurIPS 2021) proves a bandit lower bound tight up to a log factor; a search summary gives it as Omega(N/Delta + sqrt(CN/Delta)), N = number of arms, but the exact expression was not seen. With Lai-Robbins this shows the sqrt(C...) shape is near-optimal. Caveats: (1) the KL-based Lai-Robbins bound matches log T/Delta only up to constants when arm means are bounded away from 0 and 1; (2) I believe, but did not confirm in the papers, that Zimmert-Seldin's setting allows adaptive adversaries and bounds regret against corrupted losses; (3) Ito's bandit lower bound leaves a log-factor gap in the C-dependent term only, not in the K, log T or Delta gaps listed for this setting.

papers.title: Tsallis-INF: An Optimal Algorithm for Stochastic and Adversarial Bandits (Zimmert, Seldin)
papers.claim: Regret O(sum_i log T/Delta_i + sqrt(C sum_i log T/Delta_i)) in a setting that includes stochastic bandits with adversarial corruptions.

papers.title: Improved Analysis of the Tsallis-INF Algorithm in Stochastically Constrained Adversarial Bandits and Stochastic Bandits with Adversarial Corruptions (Masoudian, Seldin)
papers.claim: Replaces log T with log((K-1)T/(sum 1/Delta_i)^2) and improves the dependence on corruption C.

papers.title: On Optimal Robustness to Adversarial Corruption in Online Decision Problems (Ito)
papers.claim: Tight bound (log N)/Delta + sqrt(C log N/Delta) for experts; for bandits, a lower bound tight up to a log factor, reported in a search summary as Omega(N/Delta + sqrt(CN/Delta)) (exact form not seen), showing Tsallis-INF is nearly optimal.

triage.summary: The database's √(KT) upper bounds are out of date. For strongly observable feedback graphs, Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari and Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.15383) prove an upper bound of O(√(αT(1+ln(K/α)))). The search summary also reports an earlier √(αT ln K) bound for undirected strongly observable graphs. The same paper improves the lower bound to Ω(√(αT ln K / ln α)) for α>1, which shows a log factor is needed whenever α<K. The upper bound has a factor 1+ln(K/α) and the lower bound has log_α K. The paper says closing this log-factor gap is an open problem. Follow-up searches (2024–2026) found nothing that closes it. One 2025 paper, arXiv:2510.23992, claims optimal regret for feedback graphs, but it was seen only as a search snippet, and from that snippet it looks like a combinatorial/arm-elimination (probably stochastic) setting rather than this adversarial one. I did not check whether the upper bound needs extra assumptions (for example undirected graphs or self-loops). So the polynomial dependence √(αT) is settled, and the remaining log(K/α) versus log_α K gap is a known open problem.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Online Learning with Feedback Graphs (Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari, Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Upper bound O(√(αT(1+ln(K/α)))) for strongly observable graphs via q-Tsallis FTRL. Lower bound Ω(√(αT ln K/ln α)) for α>1. The paper says the remaining log-factor gap is an open problem.

papers.title: Online Learning with Feedback Graphs: Beyond Bandits (Alon, Cesa-Bianchi, Dekel, Koren)
papers.claim: Classifies feedback graphs by observability. In this session it appeared only as a title in a search result; its strongly observable rate was not verified.

papers.title: Nonstochastic Multi-Armed Bandits with Graph-Structured Feedback (Alon, Cesa-Bianchi, Gentile, Mannor, Mansour, Shamir)
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(√(α(G)T)) for a fixed graph once T ≥ C·α(G)^3.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed by classical results. For stochastic K-armed bandits, worst-case regret is Θ(√(KT)), so with K=2 it is Θ(√T) with no log factor either way. The database bounds (Õ(√T) upper, Ω(√T/log T) lower) are loose versions of this.

Upper bound: MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck, 2009/2010) has distribution-free regret of order √(KT) with no log factor. The 2012 survey by Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi states this in Section 4.3 ("up to a numerical constant"). I saw that statement on the survey page. Other papers in the search results quote MOSS constants of 39√(KT)+ΣΔ and 49√(KT), but I didn't confirm those in the original paper. I didn't open the original MOSS paper.

Lower bound: the same survey (Theorem 7.9, minimax lower bound) gives inf sup R_n ≥ (1/20)√(nK). The supremum is over i.i.d. {0,1}-valued (Bernoulli) reward distributions, and the setup only needs K ≥ 2. Bernoulli rewards are (1/2)-subgaussian, so this applies to the subgaussian K=2 setting and gives Ω(√T). It sits in the chapter on adversarial bandits, but the rewards in the hard instance are stochastic i.i.d. Lattimore & Szepesvári's Bandit Algorithms covers the same result in Chapter 15, §15.2 "Minimax Lower Bounds" (I only saw the table of contents, not the theorem text).

So the minimax regret for K=2 is Θ(√T). Pinning down the exact constant is a separate, finer question that isn't settled.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Theorem 7.9: minimax lower bound inf sup R_n >= (1/20) sqrt(nK) over i.i.d. {0,1}-valued reward distributions (stochastic, hence subgaussian), K>=2. Section 4.3: MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck 2010) attains regret <= const * min{sqrt(nK), (K/Δ) ln(nΔ²/K)}, i.e. O(sqrt(nK)) with no log factor.

papers.title: Minimax Policy for Heavy-tailed Bandits
papers.claim: A search snippet credits MOSS with worst-case regret 49 sqrt(KT) for the subgaussian/bounded case. I did not verify this in the paper itself.

triage.summary: For K=2, the database's upper bound (16 log(T/Δ)/Δ, from OFUL) and lower bound (log T/(2Δ)) differ only by constants. Both scale as log T / Δ, and the "poly_gap" flag on K is an artifact because K is fixed at 2. Garivier, Lattimore & Kaufmann (NeurIPS 2016) treat exactly the two-armed Gaussian case. They give fully sequential strategies with finite-time regret bounds that are asymptotically optimal, matching the Lai-Robbins constant, and minimax order-optimal; the database's log T/(2Δ) lower bound is their Theorem 6. Lattimore (JMLR 2018) gives a strategy for unit-variance Gaussian noise that is asymptotically optimal and minimax optimal up to constants, plus a finite-time lower bound that very nearly matches its upper bound. Only abstracts and summaries were seen, so the exact constants are not confirmed. Both papers assume Gaussian noise; the match carries over to subgaussian noise as worst-case bounds, since Gaussian instances are subgaussian and give the lower bound. The gap is closed.

papers.title: On Explore-Then-Commit Strategies
papers.claim: For two-armed Gaussian bandits, fully sequential strategies have finite-time regret guarantees and are asymptotically optimal and minimax order-optimal; explore-then-commit strategies are suboptimal by a factor of about 2.

papers.title: Refining the Confidence Level for Optimistic Bandit Strategies
papers.claim: For unit-variance Gaussian bandits, a strategy that is asymptotically optimal and minimax optimal up to constants, plus a finite-time lower bound for any strategy that very nearly matches its finite-time upper bound.

triage.summary: I found no published result that closes the gap for Bayesian regret (worst case over priors) in stochastic linear bandits with a fixed, arbitrary compact action set. I also found no paper that explicitly calls this Bayesian version open. The upper bound can be tightened from the database's d√T·log T (Russo & Van Roy) to d√(T log T). This rate comes from Dong & Van Roy 2018 (rate-distortion analysis of Thompson sampling); I saw the explicit form quoted by Gouverneur et al. 2025, who recover the same rate with better constants inside the log. That leaves a √(log T) gap against the d√T lower bound (Dani et al.; Lattimore–Szepesvári Theorem 24.2). Li, Wang & Zhou 2019 prove Ω(d√(T log T)), but only for action sets that change over time, so it does not apply to a fixed set. Fixed sets are settled only for special shapes: Zhang, Hadiji & Combes 2025 get minimax-optimal Θ(d√T) with no log factor for ellipsoids. Banerjee & Gopalan 2023 say earlier work called characterizing minimax regret across action spaces open, but that is the frequentist question. I could not get the text of the Lattimore–Szepesvári chapter notes to check for an explicit open-problem statement.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis for Thompson Sampling with Many Actions (Dong, Van Roy)
papers.claim: Rate-distortion analysis of Thompson sampling giving near-optimal Bayesian regret for linear bandits. Gouverneur et al. quote the rate as O(d√(T log T)), which beats the database's d√T log T upper bound.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Thompson Sampling with Infinite Action Spaces (Gouverneur, Rodriguez Gálvez, Oechtering, Skoglund)
papers.claim: Recovers the O(d√(T log T)) Bayesian regret of Thompson sampling for linear bandits with infinite action spaces and improves the constants inside the log. No log-free bound.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Li, Wang, Zhou)
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(d√(T log T)) for infinite action sets, but the sets change over time. Does not apply to a fixed compact action set.

papers.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms (Zhang, Hadiji, Combes)
papers.claim: Matching upper and lower bounds of order dσ√T (up to universal constants) for ellipsoidal action sets, with no log T. Covers only one special shape, not arbitrary compact sets.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Linear Bandits in a wide variety of Action Spaces (Banerjee, Gopalan)
papers.claim: Optimal regret lower bound for a broad class of convex action spaces. Says earlier work noted that characterizing minimax regret across action spaces was an open problem (frequentist setting).

triage.summary: The bounds come from Scheid, Boursier, Durmus et al. (arXiv 2410.17055, 2024). The upper bound is order d·sqrt(log T / T), from a 3/2-approximate G-optimal design. The lower bound is d·e^-5/(4·sqrt(T)) on the hypercube {±1/sqrt(d)}^d, for d ≥ 16 and T ≥ d². The authors say the bounds match "up to constant and logarithmic factors" but do not list removing the log factor as an open problem; their future work covers batched sampling, DPO datasets, binary search and best-arm identification links. The fetched paper page was cut off at 100,000 of about 108,000 characters, so the end was not read. Searches for follow-up papers found nothing that removes the sqrt(log T) factor in this setting. My own reasoning, not a published result: with finite K arms, the standard design plus union-bound argument gives about sqrt(d log K / T), which on the 2^d-arm hypercube is order d/sqrt(T). The gap may therefore be an artefact of the analysis, but I have not seen this worked out for logistic dueling feedback. Verdict: neither closed nor known to be open.

papers.title: Optimal Design for Reward Modeling in RLHF
papers.claim: Offline design-based selection of preference pairs. Simple regret upper bound O(d·sqrt(log T / T)) (Corollary 1) and lower bound d·e^-5/(4·sqrt(T)) on the hypercube action set (Theorem 3), stated to match up to constant and logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Active Preference Optimization for Sample Efficient RLHF
papers.claim: Active contextual preference bandit. Gives a d/sqrt(T) lower bound on the suboptimality gap for a d-dimensional hypercube action set, with nearly matching upper bounds. Related setting, does not close the gap.

triage.summary: Both bounds come from Tajdini, Scarlett & Jamieson, "Improved Regret Bounds for Linear Bandits with Heavy-Tailed Rewards" (arXiv 2506.04775, NeurIPS 2025). Upper bound (Corollary 1, MED-PE): Õ(√d · T^{1/(1+ε)} · (log n)^{ε/(1+ε)}). Lower bound (Theorem 2): Ω(T^{1/(1+ε)} · d^{ε/(1+ε)} · (log n / log d)^{ε/(1+ε)}), valid for d ≤ n ≤ 2^{⌊d/4⌋} and large T. Correction to the database entry: at ε = 1 the bounds differ only by a √(log d) factor, but for ε in (0,1) the gap in d is polynomial, d^{1/2 − ε/(1+ε)}, so 'log_gap' is only correct at ε = 1. The paper's conclusion lists "closing the remaining gap to establish true minimax-optimal rates for all moment parameters" as future work; this is general and does not single out the finite-action case. The follow-up arXiv 2508.13679 cites these bounds but does not close the stochastic finite-action gap, and I found no 2026 paper that does.

papers.title: Improved Regret Bounds for Linear Bandits with Heavy-Tailed Rewards (Tajdini, Scarlett, Jamieson)
papers.claim: Finite action sets with n arms: upper bound Õ(√d (log n)^{ε/(1+ε)} T^{1/(1+ε)}) and lower bound Ω(T^{1/(1+ε)} d^{ε/(1+ε)} (log n / log d)^{ε/(1+ε)}). The conclusion names closing the remaining gap to minimax-optimal rates for all moment parameters as future work.

papers.title: Heavy-tailed Linear Bandits: Adversarial Robustness, Best-of-both-worlds, and Beyond
papers.claim: Follow-up work on adversarial and best-of-both-worlds heavy-tailed linear bandits. Its comparison table cites the Tajdini et al. finite-arm lower bound and does not close the stochastic finite-action gap.

triage.summary: The log gap in K looks closed for the worst case over strongly observable graphs with independence number alpha: the minimax rate is Theta(sqrt(alpha*T*log(K/alpha))). Upper bound: Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari and Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023) prove O(sqrt(alpha*T*(1+ln(K/alpha)))) for strongly observable undirected graphs. It is an adversarial bound, so it also covers stochastic rewards, and it beats the database's sqrt(KT) upper bound. Lower bound: Chen, He and Zhang (ICML 2024) prove a tight Theta(sqrt(T*sum_k log(m_k+1))) for a fixed, known feedback graph made of disjoint cliques. With alpha cliques of size K/alpha this becomes Theta(sqrt(alpha*T*log(K/alpha+1))) (my derivation from the fetched abstract analysis, not read from the paper), so the database's sqrt(alpha*T) lower bound is missing a sqrt(log(K/alpha)) factor. Eldowa et al.'s own lower bound, Omega(sqrt(alpha*T*lnK/ln alpha)), uses i.i.d. Bernoulli losses but needs time-varying graphs. For fixed graphs they cite only the sqrt(alpha*T)-type bound, call the remaining log-factor gap open, and say in an appendix that the disjoint-cliques lower bound implies their algorithm is near-optimal. Caveats: (1) I did not check whether Chen et al.'s lower-bound construction uses Gaussian rewards; (2) Eldowa et al.'s upper bound assumes bounded losses, so applying it to Gaussian rewards needs a truncation argument I have not checked; (3) tight rates for every individual fixed graph remain open.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Online Learning with Feedback Graphs
papers.claim: Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari, Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023). Upper bound O(sqrt(alpha*T*(1+ln(K/alpha)))) for strongly observable undirected graphs via q-Tsallis FTRL. Lower bound Omega(sqrt(alpha*T*lnK/ln alpha)) for time-varying graphs with i.i.d. Bernoulli losses. Calls the remaining log-factor gap an open problem and cites a fixed disjoint-cliques lower bound as implying near-optimality.

papers.title: On Interpolating Experts and Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.claim: Chen, He, Zhang (ICML 2024). Tight minimax regret Theta(sqrt(T*sum_k log(m_k+1))) when arms are partitioned into groups (a fixed disjoint-cliques feedback graph). With alpha equal groups this gives Theta(sqrt(alpha*T*log(K/alpha+1))) (derived, not quoted). Extends to graph feedback via clique-cover parameters.

papers.title: Feedback graph regret bounds for Thompson Sampling and UCB
papers.claim: Lykouris, Tardos, Wali. Stochastic UCB and Thompson sampling with graph feedback get regret depending on an independent set and the gaps, with sqrt(T) worst-case dependence up to log factors.

triage.summary: Read literally, this setting has K arms, i.i.d. contexts, rewards in [0,1], no function class and no number of contexts. Without a policy class, the only well-defined benchmark is the best fixed arm, so the problem reduces to the stochastic K-armed bandit. The context can be ignored. On that reading the polylog gap is closed. MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck, COLT 2009, 'Minimax Policies for Adversarial and Stochastic Bandits') achieves O(sqrt(KT)) worst-case regret with no log factors. That matches the Ω(sqrt(KT)) lower bound already in the database (Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi survey; Foster et al.). Caveat: the database's upper bounds come from linear contextual bandit papers with d replaced by K, which looks like a mapping error. jin2026nearly is Tianyuan Jin, 'Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linear Contextual Bandits with Arbitrary Adaptive Action Sets', arXiv 2609.15170. Its Corollary 17 bound, 130[K log(2KT+1)]^{1/4} sqrt(dT log(1+T/d)), is for linear menus in R^d with adaptively chosen menus, not i.i.d. contexts. Its lower bound Ω(K^{1/4} sqrt(dT)) uses adaptive, non-i.i.d. menus. Its Corollary 2 says oblivious menus admit Õ(sqrt(dT)), which I saw only in that paper's statement. chu2011 (SupLinUCB) is also a linear-in-d result. If the intended setting is really linear contextual bandits with K arms in dimension d and stochastic contexts, then d must be a separate parameter. In that case the relevant reference points are Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019, arXiv 1904.00242): VCL-SupLinUCB has an upper bound matching their lower bound up to iterated-log factors. Their lower bound Ω(sqrt(dT log T log K)) is built with adversarial contexts. I did not find a result settling the exact log factors for i.i.d. contexts in that linear setting. My verdict of 'closed' applies only to the literal, structure-free K-armed setting given here.

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Adversarial and Stochastic Bandits
papers.claim: Audibert & Bubeck (COLT 2009): a modified UCB (MOSS) reaches the distribution-free optimal rate sqrt(nK) in stochastic bandits, with no log factor. This matches the Ω(sqrt(KT)) lower bound when contexts carry no structure.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linear Contextual Bandits with Arbitrary Adaptive Action Sets
papers.claim: Tianyuan Jin: in linear contextual bandits in R^d with K-item adaptive menus, gives E R_T ≤ 130[K log(2KT+1)]^{1/4} sqrt(dT log(1+T/d)) (Cor. 17) and Ω(K^{1/4} sqrt(dT)) for T ≥ d² with adaptive (non-i.i.d.) menus. Cor. 2 says oblivious menus admit Õ(sqrt(dT)). This is the source of the database's upper bound, with d replaced by K.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits
papers.claim: Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019): lower bound Ω(sqrt(dT log T log n)) for n ≤ 2^{d/2} actions, built from adversarial context sequences. The VCL-SupLinUCB upper bound matches it up to iterated-log factors. Relevant only if the setting is really linear with a separate d.

triage.summary: The gap is closed: the minimax regret is Theta(sqrt(KT)). The database's upper bound sqrt(KT log T) comes from a UCB-style analysis. MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck 2009) is cited in search results as achieving O(sqrt(KT)) worst-case regret with known horizon; its original analysis was for bounded rewards. Lattimore's Optimally Confident UCB (arXiv:1507.07880) is stated for K arms with subgaussian noise and gets order-optimal worst-case regret O(sqrt(KT)) together with optimal problem-dependent regret. Its anytime follow-up (arXiv:1603.08661) is also described as reaching the minimax rate without knowing T. kl-UCB++ (arXiv:1702.07211) is both minimax and asymptotically optimal. The Lattimore-Szepesvari book's chapter 'The UCB Algorithm: Minimax Optimality' covers MOSS. Combined with the classical Omega(sqrt(KT)) lower bound, the rate is tight with no log factor. Caveat: I did not open the PDFs, so theorem statements and constants come from search snippets; I could not confirm the book's exact constant.

papers.title: Optimally Confident UCB: Improved Regret for Finite-Armed Bandits (Lattimore)
papers.claim: For K-armed bandits with subgaussian noise, achieves order-optimal worst-case regret O(sqrt(KT)) together with order-optimal problem-dependent regret.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of the Anytime Optimally Confident UCB Algorithm (Lattimore)
papers.claim: Anytime algorithm described as achieving the minimax rate, as MOSS does, but without knowing the horizon in advance.

papers.title: A minimax and asymptotically optimal algorithm for stochastic bandits (Menard & Garivier)
papers.claim: kl-UCB++ is minimax optimal (O(sqrt(KT))) and asymptotically optimal; credits MOSS (Audibert & Bubeck 2009) with minimax regret O(sqrt(KT)).

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems (Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Survey presenting MOSS's O(sqrt(KT)) upper bound and the matching Omega(sqrt(KT)) lower bound.

triage.summary: The gap is closed: the √log K factor in the database's upper bounds comes from Exp3-style analyses and was removed in 2009. Audibert & Bubeck (COLT 2009) introduced INF (Implicitly Normalized Forecaster), which achieves O(√(KT)) regret for adversarial K-armed bandits; the abstract says this closes the logarithmic gap with the Ω(√(KT)) lower bound. I only saw abstracts and fragments, not the theorem statements or constants. The JMLR 2010 follow-up ('Regret Bounds and Minimax Policies under Partial Monitoring') covers the same result in general form. Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, JMLR 2021) also achieves optimal pseudo-regret within constants without knowing the horizon; the exact constant (believed to be about 4√(KT)) was not visible in the results. Both upper bounds are for pseudo-regret, which equals expected regret against an oblivious adversary. With the Ω(√(KT)) lower bound from Auer et al. 2002, the minimax rate is Θ(√(KT)).

triage.summary:
The polynomial gap in K has been closed for a long time. The database's upper bound, inherited from Lee et al. 2020 (Theorem 3.1), grows like K^2.5. That is very loose for plain K-armed adversarial bandits. Exp3.P (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund & Schapire 2002) already guarantees high-probability regret of O(sqrt(KT log(K/δ))). The Bubeck–Cesa-Bianchi survey (Theorem 3.10 there) states this as about 5.15·sqrt(nK ln(K/δ)) with probability at least 1−δ, when the tuning is chosen using δ. Neu (2015), with Exp3-IX, gets O(sqrt(KT log K) + sqrt(KT/log K)·log(1/δ)) without forced exploration, and that bound holds for any δ.

Losses in [-1,1] reduce to [0,1] by the affine map (x+1)/2, which changes regret by only a factor of 2. So these bounds apply to the bounded_pm1 setting. The upper bound sqrt(KT log(K/δ)) matches the lower bound sqrt(T(K−1) log(1/(4δ)))/27 from Gerchinovitz & Lattimore 2016 up to a sqrt(log K) factor, and possibly constants. The K exponent is therefore tight at 1/2, and so is the T exponent. Only logarithmic factors in K remain open.

I saw these bounds in search results, not in the papers themselves. I did not check the exact theorem numbers or constants in the original papers.

triage.summary:
I'm treating this as closed, but only up to iterated-log factors and only under one reading of the setting. The database entry is internally inconsistent. Its upper bounds come from linear contextual bandit papers (SupLinUCB; Jin 2026). These seem to have been instantiated with the dimension d set equal to K. The Jin-derived formula then scales as K^{3/4}·√T, not the K^{1/2} listed in per_var.

**If the setting is the standard finite-arm linear contextual bandit with arbitrary (oblivious) adversarial contexts:** Li, Wang and Zhou (COLT 2019, arXiv 1904.00242) settle the T-dependence. They prove a lower bound of Ω(√(dT·log T·log n)) for n ≤ 2^{d/2} actions, needing T ≥ d(log n)^{1+ε}. They also give an algorithm, Variable-Confidence-Level SupLinUCB, whose regret matches this up to iterated-log factors. This lower bound is a √log T factor stronger than the database's √(KT). The upper bound is also better than SupLinUCB's log^{3/2} factor. With d = n = K the minimax rate is Θ̃(√(KT·log K·log T)), up to loglog factors. So the T log-gap is closed up to iterated logs: the true rate has an extra √log T over the database's lower bound. One caveat: I only saw the abstract-level claim that the upper bound matches up to iterated-log factors, not the exact theorem. I also did not confirm the paper's exact assumption on how contexts are chosen.

**If action sets may adapt to the unknown parameter and history (Jin 2026, arXiv 2609.15170):** the K- and d-dependence changes. For K ≥ d the minimax rate is Θ̃(√(dT)·min{√d, (d log K)^{1/4}}). For 2 ≤ K ≤ d it is Θ̃(K^{1/4}√(dT)), with the lower bound needing T ≥ d². Here the bounds match only up to unspecified log factors, so the exact log-T power for this variant is not pinned down.

**If the rewards don't depend on the context at all (just an i.i.d. K-armed bandit):** the problem reduces to a standard multi-armed bandit, where the minimax rate is the √(KT) order. I did not check a source for this reading.

The database should fix the d = K substitution and the K exponent in per_var.

triage.summary:
Setting: stochastic K-armed bandits where the set of available arms changes over time and may be chosen adversarially (stochastic sleeping bandits). The benchmark is the best available arm in each round, which is the same as the best fixed ordering of the arms.

**What is established**
- Lower bound: Ω(√(KT)). Gaillard–Saha–Dan (AISTATS 2023) and Saha–Gaillard–Valko (ICML 2020) both cite this rate for the stochastic-reward, adversarial-availability case.
- Upper bound: I found no paper that achieves √(KT) here without a log factor. I also found no paper that states the log gap as an open problem.

**Database upper bound can be improved (my own argument, not a citation)**
Plain UCB, restricted to the arms available in each round, appears to give O(√(KT log T)):
- On the event that all confidence bounds hold, the per-round regret is at most UCB(a_t) − μ(a_t) ≤ 2√(2 log T / n_{a_t}).
- Summing over each arm's pull counts gives O(√(KT log T)).

This is tighter than the database's best upper bound, which carries a log^{3/4}·(log)^{1/2} factor. If it holds, the remaining gap is √(log T).

**What I could not verify**
- Whether MOSS-style techniques remove the last √log T factor when availability is adversarial. No source I saw addressed this.
- The exact stochastic bounds in Kleinberg–Niculescu-Mizil–Sharma (COLT 2008 / MLJ 2010). Fetching the PDF failed (certificate rejected), and the page I could open had no abstract. A separate listing quoted the abstract as claiming bounds that are optimal "up to a constant or a sub-logarithmic factor", but I didn't see the specific theorems.

**Verdict: blank.** I found no paper that closes the gap and none that explicitly calls it open.

triage.summary: Closed up to a sqrt(log T) factor. The upper bound comes from Zimmert & Lattimore (COLT 2022): the minimax regret for adaptive adversarial linear bandits with general action sets, including convex bodies, is O(d sqrt(T log T)), and it holds with high probability. This is computationally inefficient; their efficient entropic-barrier FTRL gets about d^2 sqrt(T) log T, improving Lee et al. 2020's d^{7/2} sqrt(T). The lower bound is Omega(d sqrt T) on the hypercube, which is a convex body: Shamir (arXiv:1408.2368) gives c(d-1) sqrt(T), seen in a search snippet, and Dani-Hayes-Kakade 2007 show the bandit/full-information gap is at least sqrt(n), seen in the abstract only. So the d-exponent is 1 on both sides; the database's d^2.5 upper and sqrt(dT) lower bounds are both outdated. I read abstracts and snippets, not full papers, and did not check that Shamir's loss scaling rescales to rewards in [0,1]. A gap of order d remains if only polynomial-time algorithms are allowed.

triage.summary:
The polynomial gap in d is closed, up to logarithmic factors. The database's upper bound, inherited from Lee et al. 2020, scales as d^2·ϑ·√(dT). The database's lower bound scales as √(dT). Both are stale.

**Upper bound:** Zimmert and Lattimore (COLT 2022, "Return of the bias") give an agent for adversarial linear bandits against an adaptive adversary on general action sets. According to the PMLR page and full text, its regret is O(d√(T log(T/δ))) with probability at least 1−δ. Their minimax bound is O(d√(T log T)), and they state that for general action sets the minimax regret is the same against adaptive and oblivious adversaries. That algorithm is not computationally efficient. Their efficient version (FTRL with the entropic barrier) has regret O(d²√T log T) against an adaptive adversary.

**Lower bound:** The hypercube is a convex body, and it already forces Ω(d√T) expected regret. One search result I saw (arXiv 1408.2368, "On the Complexity of Bandit Linear Optimization") states this for T ≥ d⁴/4. Cesa-Bianchi and Kakade (arXiv 1110.4322) also say the order-d√T rate cannot be improved in general. An expected-regret lower bound of this order also rules out a better high-probability bound for constant δ.

**Result:** For worst-case regret over convex bodies, the rate in d is Θ(d), and the rate in T is √T (√(log T) in the upper bound). The δ-dependence is also close: the upper bound grows with √(log(1/δ)), which the √(log(1/δ)) term in Bacchiocchi et al. 2026 matches. A gap of more than log factors remains only for computationally efficient algorithms (d² versus d). Separately, for convex bodies with self-concordance parameter ϑ, the gap stays open if you need bounds that adapt to ϑ.

I did not see the original Dani–Hayes–Kakade hypercube construction in this session. The hypercube lower bound rests on the 1408.2368 snippet and the Cesa-Bianchi–Kakade statement.

triage.summary:
The √log K gap is closed, but only by combining two published results. I did not find a paper that states the contextual bound itself.

Setting: M_ctx finite contexts chosen by an oblivious adversary, K arms, rewards in [0,1]. The database upper bound, √(2·K·M·T·log K), comes from running a separate Exp3 for each context.

**Upper bound without the log factor.** Replace Exp3 with Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, arXiv 1807.07623). Its Theorem 1 bounds adversarial pseudo-regret by 4√(KT)+1 with importance-weighted estimators. The bound is anytime: the learning rate is η_t = 2/√t, so it needs neither T nor a doubling scheme. That matters here because each context's round count T_c is unknown in advance. Running one copy per context gives regret at most Σ_c(4√(K·T_c)+1). By Cauchy–Schwarz this is at most 4√(K·M·T)+M, which is O(√(KMT)) when T ≥ M. Against an oblivious adversary, pseudo-regret and expected regret coincide. Audibert & Bubeck's INF (COLT 2009 / JMLR 2010) already removed the √log K factor for the non-contextual problem.

**Matching lower bound.** Split the rounds into M blocks of T/M, one block per context, and apply the existing √((K−1)T)/504 bound to each block. This gives Ω(√(MKT)). Note that the lower bounds in the database omit the M factor.

So the minimax rate is Θ(√(KMT)): it is tight in K, M and T up to constants.

**Caveats.**
- I found no paper that explicitly states the composed O(√(KMT)) bound for this setting.
- I could not read the text of Lattimore & Szepesvári Chapter 18 ("One bandit per context"). The fetched PDF came back as unreadable binary, so I could not check whether the book makes this remark or poses it as an exercise.
- Neither of the two composition steps is spelled out in a paper I found. The anytime per-context argument and the block-splitting lower bound are my own reasoning. They are standard arguments, but I have not seen them written down this session.

triage.summary:
The bounds in this cell come from static adversarial linear bandits on the unit ℓ2 ball. They do not depend on the number of switches. The question is whether the √log T gap between the Θ(√(dT)) lower bound and the O(√(dT log T)) upper bound has been closed. I found no paper that closes it and no paper that explicitly calls it an open problem.

- **Lower bound, Jacobsen–Baudry–Ito–Cesa-Bianchi (arXiv:2603.28201, 2026):** They prove the "folklore Θ̃(√(dT))" minimax rate on the Euclidean ball. Their lower bound (Thm 5.2) carries a factor √(d/(d∨log T)), so it is only Ω(√(dT)) when d ≳ log T. For the upper bound they cite Bubeck et al. 2012 as Õ(√(dT)), with the logs hidden. They do not say whether removing the log is open.
- **Upper bound, Bubeck–Cohen–Li (arXiv:1711.01037, AISTATS 2018), Theorem 3:** On ℓp balls with p∈(1,2] they get R_T ≤ 2^{6/(p−1)}√(nT log T). This keeps the √log T and, at p=2, gives the same rate as Bubeck et al. 2012, so it does not close the gap.
- **FTPL papers (Lévy et al. COLT 2026, arXiv:2510.24187; arXiv:2610.17818):** Their bounds on the ball are only O(d√(T log T)), worse than the bound already in the database.

The gap appears unresolved, but I found no explicit "open problem" statement, so the verdict is blank.

The DB's upper bound is loose relative to the literature. Phased elimination with G-optimal design (Lattimore–Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms, Ch. 22) is commonly cited as giving O(sqrt(dT log(KT))), i.e. T-dependence sqrt(T log T) rather than sqrt(T)·log^{3/4}T; I did not fetch the theorem text. The Li–Wang–Zhou (COLT 2019) lower bound Omega(sqrt(dT log T log K)), K ≤ 2^{d/2}, is for time-varying (contextual, adversarially chosen in advance) action sets; the HTML text says its hard instances vary across rounds, so it does not settle the fixed-set case. The remaining gap is whether sqrt(dT log K) without log T is achievable under subgaussian noise, versus a matching fixed-set lower bound of order sqrt(dT log T) or sqrt(dT log K). triage.summary:
I could not find a published result that closes this gap exactly for i.i.d. stochastic contexts, and none that calls it open. The literature does, however, narrow the gap well beyond what the database records.

(1) Upper bound. Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019, arXiv:1904.00242) give a Variable-Confidence-Level SupLinUCB algorithm for finite-action linear contextual bandits (n ≤ 2^{d/2} actions per round). Its regret matches their lower bound of Ω(√(dT log T log n)) up to iterated-logarithm factors, so the upper bound is about √(dT log T log K)·polyloglog. Action sets in that analysis may be chosen arbitrarily, so the upper bound should also cover stochastic contexts. It is much tighter than the database's best upper bound, √(Td)·log(2Td)·min(√d, (d log K)^{1/4}), from jin2026nearly.

(2) Lower bound. Li et al.'s Ω(√(dT log T log K)) is built from "delicately constructed adversarial sequences" of action sets, according to the abstract. It is therefore unclear whether it holds when contexts are i.i.d. Ito (NeurIPS 2024) proves an O(√(dT log(K·min{1, S/d}))) upper bound with a matching lower bound for contextual linear bandits, where S is the size of the context space. For S ≥ d this gives Θ(√(dT log K)). That improves the database's √(dT) lower bound by a √(log K) factor, if Ito's setting fits this one. I believe Ito's model uses i.i.d. contexts, possibly with adversarial losses, but I could not confirm this: the PDF did not extract and the abstracts don't describe how contexts are generated.

Net result: the remaining gap is at most about √(log T)·polyloglog between √(dT log K) and √(dT log T log K), not the log^{3/4} T gap the database shows. Whether the extra √(log T) is needed under i.i.d. contexts was not settled by any paper I found. Tool note: the Ito PDF fetch returned unreadable binary, so this verdict relies only on what the abstracts state.

triage.summary:
The polynomial gap in d is closed by published work, but a √log T gap in T remains, and I found no paper that resolves it.

**The gap in d is closed.** The database's best lower bound, √(dT), is too weak. The standard minimax lower bound for stochastic linear bandits with a fixed infinite action set is Ω(d√T). Sources:
- Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis (2010), for the unit ball.
- Lattimore & Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms* (2020), Theorem 24.2: unit ball, 1-sub-Gaussian noise, valid when T ≥ d²/48. The hypercube Theorem 24.1 is from memory; I did not check it this session.
- Dani, Hayes & Kakade (COLT 2008), cited as the original source.
- Zhang, Hadiji & Combes (2025): for ellipsoid action sets, a lower bound of order min(dσ√T + d‖θ‖_A, ‖θ‖_A T) and an algorithm matching it up to a universal constant. So for ellipsoids, including the unit ball, the minimax rate is Θ(d√T) with no log factor.
- Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (2011) also note that d√T cannot be improved in general.

The worst case over arbitrary compact sets includes the unit ball, so the lower bound is Ω(d√T). That matches the upper bound's linear dependence on d. The upper bound in the database (Dani et al. 2008 with δ=1/T) is d√T times polylog(T). Known methods reduce it to about d√(T log T), for example phased elimination over a cover or Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade's d√T up to logs.

**Caveats.**
- The lower-bound proofs I saw use sub-Gaussian (Gaussian) noise. The problem specifies rewards in [0,1]. Rescaled constructions with Bernoulli rewards are standard, and the database's own Ω(√(dT)) lower bound is already inherited across this difference, but I did not see a [0,1]-specific statement this session.
- The lower bound needs T ≳ d².

**What remains open: a √log T gap.** It sits between d√(T log T) and d√T for general (non-ellipsoidal) fixed compact action sets in the frequentist worst case. No paper I found closes it.
- Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019) prove √(dT log T log n) bounds for finite, contextual (time-varying) action sets. Per a search-result summary, their infinite-set bound is d√(T log T)·poly(log log T), and their abstract says tight bounds for infinite action sets remain open. I only confirmed that wording for the finite-set version, and that setting has time-varying sets, not this fixed-set one.
- Gouverneur et al. (2024) get O(d√T) via chaining, but only as Bayesian regret and under a reward-continuity assumption.

Because the poly(d) gap is resolved, the verdict is "closed", with this residual log(T) gap noted.

triage.summary:
I found no published result that closes this gap. The gap itself is stated explicitly in the paper that gives the upper bound. One label in the database seems to be wrong.

**Where the upper bound comes from.** The cited upper bound, bai2021sample Theorem 5, is Bai, Jin, Wang & Xiong, "Sample-Efficient Learning of Stackelberg Equilibria in General-Sum Games" (NeurIPS 2021, arXiv 2102.11494). I read the theorem list in the ar5iv version. Theorem 5 is not about K-armed bandits. It is an Õ(d²/ε²) upper bound for learning Stackelberg equilibria in linear bandit games, where d is the feature dimension. The database appears to have recorded d as "K".

**The gap is acknowledged in the same paper.** Appendix E.2 adapts the paper's bandit-game lower bound to get Ω(d/ε²) for linear bandit games. The authors say the upper bound is off from this "by at most an Õ(d) factor". That is the K² (really d²) versus K (really d) gap in the database.

**What I could not find.**
- No later paper in my searches tightens the linear-bandit Stackelberg rate to d/ε² or raises the lower bound to d²/ε².
- I could not identify li2023tight, the claimed source of the lower bound. In any case, Bai et al. already give an Ω(d/ε²) lower bound for this setting.
- I could not find a formal statement calling this an open problem. It is "known open" only in the sense that the authors explicitly flag the gap.

**If you meant the plain finite-action setting.** For the setting the database labels as K-armed (finite action sets, bandit feedback), the same paper is tight. Theorem 2 gives an Õ(AB/ε²) upper bound and Theorem 3 a matching Ω(AB/ε²) lower bound, where A and B are the two players' action counts. If the intended setting is a Stackelberg bandit game with A = B = K, the gap is closed at K²/ε².

**Checking limits.** The PDF fetches returned unreadable binary, so I took the theorem statements from the ar5iv HTML version. That page's answer covered only the first 100k of its 185k characters, but the theorem list and the Appendix E.2 remark were both readable there.

triage.summary: The gap is closed up to log factors. Luo, Tong, Zhang & Zhang (ALT 2023, arXiv:2210.01376) explicitly allow an adaptive adversary that picks the loss l_t and graph G_t based on the learner's past actions, with G_t revealed only after the action for strongly observable graphs (the 'uninformed setting'). Their Theorem 3 gives, with probability at least 1-6δ, Reg ≤ Õ(√(Σ_t α_t log(1/δ)) + max_t α_t log(1/δ)). The tuning uses knowledge of α_t; the paper says a doubling trick removes this. For a fixed graph this is Õ(√(αT)+α), matching the existing Ω(√(αT)) lower bounds (Mannor-Shamir 2011, Alon et al. 2015). The K-exponent gap (upper 0.5 vs lower 0) is an artifact of writing the uppers in K and the lowers in α. Worst case over graphs, the K-armed bandit (α=K) is a strongly observable instance, so the lower bound is Ω(√(KT)), matching the √(KT) uppers. I could not read the full PDFs of Kocák et al. 2014 or Neu 2015; per Luo et al., Neu 2015's bound had poly(K) dependence and needed self-loops on every node.

For strongly observable feedback graphs, published upper bounds scale as √(αT) up to logs. Up to logarithmic factors, the gap is closed. It mostly comes from the bounds being stated in different terms. The upper bounds in the database depend on K, while the lower bound depends on the independence number α of the graph. That is why K looks poly-gapped (exponent 0.5 vs 0).

- **Expected regret, any fixed loss sequence:** Alon, Cesa-Bianchi, Dekel & Koren (COLT 2015, arXiv 1502.07617), Theorem 2(i), give Exp3.G with regret O(√(αT)·ln(KT)) on strongly observable graphs. Their extension to time-varying graphs gives O(√(ᾱT)·ln(KT)), where ᾱ is the average of the per-round α_t. Since Exp3.G uses the graph only after the action is chosen, revealing it after the action is fine. This matches the Ω(√(αT)) lower bound up to log factors.
- **Adaptive adversary:** Alon et al. assume a loss sequence fixed in advance. For the adaptive case, Luo, Tong, Zhang & Zhang (ALT 2023, arXiv 2210.01376) give a high-probability bound of about Õ(√(Σ_t α_t) + max_t α_t) for time-varying strongly observable graphs, with no poly(K) dependence. High-probability bounds of this kind usually carry over to adaptive adversaries, but I did not check this paper's adversary assumptions.
- **Log factors (undirected graphs):** Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari & Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2305.15383) give an upper bound of O(√(αT(1+ln(K/α)))) using q-Tsallis FTRL. They also prove a lower bound of Ω(√(αT·ln K/ln α)) for α>1, which shows some log factor is needed whenever α<K. I did not confirm that this bound covers directed or time-varying graphs.

Caveat: the polynomial dependence is settled. What remains open is the exact log factor for directed and time-varying graphs, which is a minor log-level question.

So the polynomial K-gap (upper exponent 0.5 vs. lower 0) disappears once the upper bound is stated in terms of alpha ≤ K: both sides are sqrt(alpha T) up to logs. Only a small log-factor gap remains, in the regime 1 < alpha < K.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed up to logarithmic factors. It looks polynomial in K only because the database's upper bounds are bandit bounds of order sqrt(KT) (Tsallis-INF style), which ignore the graph. The lower bound is of order sqrt(alpha_G T), where alpha_G is the graph's independence number (the size of its largest set of arms with no edges between them).

- **Alon, Cesa-Bianchi, Dekel and Koren (COLT 2015, arXiv 1502.07617):** this paper is already in the database, but only its lower bound is used there. Its abstract states that the minimax regret for strongly observable graphs is Theta~(sqrt(alpha T)). The matching upper bound, of order sqrt(alpha T log K), is missing from the database. It covers directed graphs too.
- **Eldowa, Esposito, Cesari and Cesa-Bianchi (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2305.15383):** for strongly observable undirected graphs they sharpen the upper bound to O(sqrt(alpha T (1 + ln(K/alpha)))). They also prove a lower bound of Omega(sqrt(alpha T ln K / ln alpha)) for alpha > 1, which shows a log factor is needed whenever alpha < K. Only a log-level gap remains, and only for intermediate alpha.

So the K exponent is closed: as a function of alpha the rate is sqrt(alpha T), up to logs.

One caveat: I did not check the theorem statements for whether these bounds are stated for adaptive adversaries. Upper bounds for Exp3-type and FTRL methods (the algorithm families behind these results) usually hold as pseudo-regret against adaptive adversaries, but that is an assumption here, not something I confirmed.

triage.summary: The database's polynomial gap is an artifact of stating the upper bound in K. For strongly observable graphs, Alon et al. (2015) already give O(sqrt(alpha T)·log(KT)). Eldowa et al. (NeurIPS 2023) improve this to O(sqrt(alpha T (1+ln(K/alpha)))) and also prove a lower bound of Omega(sqrt(alpha T ln K / ln alpha)) for alpha>1. Together these match the database's Omega(sqrt(alpha T)) lower bound up to logarithmic factors, so the gap is closed in polynomial terms. A log-factor gap remains between 1+ln(K/alpha) and ln K/ln alpha for intermediate alpha; according to search summaries (paper not opened), the authors describe it as open. Searches of 2024-2025 work found nothing that closes this log gap in the standard K-armed setting.

triage.summary: No paper I found closes the √log T gap for this exact setting (sub-Gaussian noise, known σ, adaptive per-path corruption, regret against uncorrupted means), and none says it is open. Nearby results strongly suggest the extra log factor can be removed. (1) For losses in [0,1], Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin 2021) gets O(√(KT)) adversarial regret, and its self-bounding regime explicitly includes stochastic bandits with adversarial corruptions. My own inference, not stated in the papers: switching to the uncorrupted reference costs at most 2C, giving O(√(KT)+C), which matches the Ω(√(KT)) lower bound. That covers bounded rewards, not sub-Gaussian noise. (2) For heavy-tailed noise, HTINF/AdaTINF (Huang, Dai & Huang 2022) get O(σ K^{1-1/α} T^{1/α}) with no log factor even adversarially; with α=2 that is O(σ√(KT)). I only saw the abstract, so I could not check whether its adversarial model covers adaptive corruption added to sub-Gaussian noise, or whether it needs extra assumptions such as truncated non-negativity. The corrupted-bandit papers I found (Lykouris et al. 2018, Gupta et al. 2019, CRIMED, HuberUCB) give gap-dependent or problem-dependent bounds with log factors.

triage.summary: The gap is an artifact of a weak inherited lower bound (log T from Bubeck et al. 2013), not an open problem. The setting allows zero corruption (C=0), so it contains the ordinary uncorrupted 2-armed Gaussian bandit with known sigma. That problem has a standard worst-case minimax lower bound of Omega(sqrt(KT)), i.e. Omega(sqrt(T)) for K=2 (Lattimore & Szepesvari 2020, Ch. 15; arXiv 2608.17841 places the Gaussian construction in Exercise 15.2; I did not fetch the book chapter itself). The upper bound O(sqrt(T log T)) from Bogunovic et al. 2020 (Thm 2) is therefore tight in T up to a sqrt(log T) factor. The polynomial gap in T is closed and the rate is Theta(sqrt(T)) up to logs. A regret lower bound of about C for large C is folklore; I did not search for a source. Removing the last sqrt(log T) factor (O(sqrt(T)+C) against an adaptive adversary on uncorrupted means, e.g. via Tsallis-INF, which gets O(sqrt(KT)) adversarial regret for bounded losses) is a minor log-factor question. I did not check whether it carries over to unbounded Gaussian rewards.

triage.summary: For the worst case over graph sequences, the gap is closed by a classical result. The class allows any oblivious sequence of strongly observable, never-revealed graphs, including one where every arm has only a self-loop. That sequence is exactly the plain K-armed bandit, so the Lai-Robbins (1985) lower bound applies: liminf R(T)/log T >= sum_{i suboptimal} Delta_i/KL_i (Burnetas-Katehakis for general [0,1] rewards). This matches the existing KL-UCB / K_inf upper bounds sum Delta_i/kl_i * log T, with Theta(1/Delta) per arm summed over about K arms. The poly gap in Delta and K is therefore an artifact of the database's weak log(T) lower-bound entry (caron2012leveraging). I saw the Lai-Robbins statement only in secondary sources (arXiv 2001.11201, Wikipedia), not the original theorem text, so constants and the KL convention should be checked against the DOI. Caveat: if the target is a graph-adaptive bound (in terms of the independence numbers alpha_t), that is a different question. Lykouris-Tardos-Wali (ALT 2020) give gap- and graph-dependent UCB/TS bounds that don't use the graph to choose arms; I couldn't parse the PDF, so their exact form is unconfirmed. Cohen-Hazan-Koren (ICML 2016) give sqrt(alpha T) for stochastic losses with hidden graphs. I found no matching alpha-dependent instance-dependent lower bound for time-varying, never-revealed graphs, so that refinement appears open.

This applies here because a sequence of self-loop-only graphs (strongly observable) reduces the problem to the plain bandit. It matches KL-UCB.

triage.summary:
Verdict: closed, with one caveat below.

**Why it is closed.** The database's best lower bound is a bare Ω(log T) with no dependence on the gaps Δ or on K. That is too weak, and it is the only reason a gap shows up. The setting allows any strongly observable graph sequence. That includes a fixed graph, and it includes the graph with only self-loops, which is the ordinary bandit. So the classical Lai–Robbins bound applies, at least in the worst case over the class: Ω(Σ_i log T/Δ_i) in the Gaussian/Bernoulli kl form. This matches UCB1 / KL-UCB in both Δ and K up to constants.

**Fixed graphs.** Here the asymptotic instance-dependent rate is fully characterised by the optimal value of a graph-dependent linear program (LP):
- Buccapatnam, Eryilmaz & Shroff (arXiv 1704.07943) derive this LP lower bound for uniformly good policies. Their UCB-type and randomized policies match it up to a constant factor.
- Wu, György & Szepesvári (NeurIPS 2015, arXiv 1510.08108) give non-asymptotic problem-dependent lower bounds that recover the asymptotic ones, plus algorithms that match them up to a universal constant.
- Marinov, Mohri & Zimmert (NeurIPS 2022, arXiv 2206.10022) show that "optimal finite-time regret" is not uniquely defined for feedback graphs. For their notion, they give an algorithm that is quasi-optimal both in finite time and asymptotically.

Together, the Δ and K exponents (upper 1 vs. lower 0) are pinned down: the right order is a graph-dependent sum of terms log T/Δ_i, between the independence-number and domination-number scales. The database simply lacks these lower bounds.

**Caveat.** I found no paper that exactly characterises the instance-dependent rate for arbitrary time-varying oblivious graph sequences known in advance. Lykouris, Tardos & Wali (ALT 2020, arXiv 1905.09898) give graph-and-gap-dependent UCB/Thompson-sampling upper bounds. Their abstract does not say whether time-varying graphs are covered, and I did not read the full paper. Mehta (arXiv 2305.04093) sharpens the UCB-N/TS-N analysis for undirected graphs. Read per instance, the exact constant for time-varying sequences may still be open. The polynomial gap in Δ and K as recorded, however, is closed by the known lower bounds.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed. The Ω(√T/log T) lower bound in the database is just weak. The classic minimax lower bound Ω(√(KT)) applies here, and for K=2 it gives Ω(√T). That matches Exp3's O(√(T log 2)) = O(√T) up to constants.

Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi (2012, arXiv 1204.5721), Theorem 3.4 in Section 3.3, gives a lower bound of (1/20)·√(nK) for any forecaster. It is built from i.i.d. Bernoulli rewards: one arm has mean 1/2 and another has mean 1/2+√(K/n), with n the horizon (T here). Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund & Schapire (SIAM J. Comput. 2002) earlier proved a matching lower bound of order √(KT). Stochastic i.i.d. rewards are a special case of an oblivious adversary, which in turn is a special case of an adaptive one. So the lower bound carries over to the adaptive K=2 setting, for both pseudo-regret and expected regret.

One caveat: if "regret" against an adaptive adversary meant policy regret, the rates would differ (e.g. T^{2/3} with switching costs). The database's upper bounds come from the standard Exp3 regret, though, so the standard notion applies.

I couldn't extract the theorem statement from the Auer et al. PDF (the fetch returned binary content). The constant 1/20 and the theorem number come from search snippets of the Bubeck–Cesa-Bianchi survey. A 2016 paper (arXiv 1608.02732) quotes the constant as 1/24. Either way the order is √(KT).

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Theorem 3.4 (Sec. 3.3), per search snippets: a minimax lower bound of (1/20)·√(nK) for any forecaster, built from Bernoulli rewards. Since adversaries include stochastic environments, this gives Ω(√T) for K=2 and matches Exp3 up to constants.

papers.claim: From the abstract: Exp3's per-round payoff approaches the best arm's at rate O(T^{-1/2}), and a matching lower bound shows this is the best possible. That is regret Θ(√(KT)) against adversaries.

triage.summary: For full-information K-expert adversarial regret with losses in [0,1], the minimax worst-case regret is known to be Θ(√(T log K)), with matching constants. Hedge with η=√(8 ln K/T) gets regret ≤ √((T/2) ln K) (Freund–Schapire; stated in arXiv:1307.8187 and arXiv:1904.07272). The i.i.d. Bernoulli(1/2) loss construction gives a lower bound of about √((T/2) ln K) for any algorithm (Cesa-Bianchi et al. 1997; Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi 2006). I saw this attribution only in a search summary and did not open either source. Gravin–Peres–Sivan 2016 also show MW's regret is exactly √(T ln K/2) and give a (2/3)√(T ln K/2) lower bound for broad MW families. The database's √(KT) upper bounds are bandit bounds carried over to full information, so they are loose. The √(T log K) lower bound already matches the right order, and the gap is closed.

triage.summary: I couldn't verify a published result that closes this gap: most PDFs I fetched came back unreadable (Bubeck's lecture notes, the UW lecture notes, the arXiv PDF of Srebro et al.). The database bounds are inherited from other settings: the upper bound d^2·vartheta·sqrt(T log T) from a bandit paper, the lower bound sqrt(T log d) from ito2021optimal. My own reasoning, not checked against any source: (1) running exponential weights over the whole convex body should give regret of order d·log T/eta + eta·T, i.e. O(sqrt(dT log T)), when |<x,y>| <= 1. Bubeck's 2011 notes have a chapter on this algorithm, but I never saw the rate. A 2026 arXiv snippet gives O(sqrt(dT log T)) for losses in [0,1], possibly in a different setting. (2) On the hypercube, whose polar loss set is the l1 ball, an adversary playing ±e_i with random signs, cycling through coordinates, splits the game into d one-dimensional games of T/d rounds, giving Omega(sqrt(dT)) for T >= d. I found no source stating this. If both hold, the rate is Theta(sqrt(dT)) up to sqrt(log T) and the database gap is an artifact of inherited bounds. Srebro, Sridharan & Tewari (2011) tie the minimax regret to the 'martingale type' of the action and loss sets, but the parts I read give no explicit d-dimensional sqrt(dT) statement. Audibert–Bubeck–Lugosi's full-information bound m·sqrt(n log(d/m)) uses losses in [0,1]^d, not the polar normalization. Verdict is blank because none of these claims was confirmed from a source.

triage.summary:
The gap is already closed by classical results. It looks like an artifact of an incomplete database. The full-information K-armed adversarial problem (prediction with expert advice, losses in [-1,1]) has minimax regret Θ(sqrt(T log K)).

- **Upper bound:** Hedge (exponential weights / Multiplicative Weights) gets regret O(sqrt(T log K)). For losses in [0,1] this is sqrt(T ln K / 2), and rescaling to [-1,1] only changes the constant.
- **Lower bound:** The database already lists Ω(sqrt(T log K)), the first term of the Min in ito2021optimal Theorem 5 (the worst case over Delta).

**Why the database shows a gap:** Its upper bounds carry an extra sqrt(K) factor. 2·sqrt(3)·sqrt(KT log K) is the bandit-feedback rate from bubeck2012minimax, inherited into full information. It is not the right rate for full information.

**Supporting results found in this session:**
- Gravin, Peres and Sivan (ICALP 2017, arXiv 1607.02834) show the Multiplicative Weights algorithm's regret is exactly sqrt(T ln k / 2). Their abstract says this completely closes the gap between upper and lower bounds. They also give a (2/3)·sqrt(T ln k / 2) lower bound for a broader family of algorithms with time-varying or randomized learning rates.
- Slivkins' book "Introduction to Multi-Armed Bandits" (arXiv 1904.07272) covers Hedge in the full-feedback setting.
- The classical asymptotically tight minimax bound in the experts setting is by Cesa-Bianchi, Freund, Haussler, Helmbold, Schapire and Warmuth ("How to use expert advice", JACM 1997). This search did not return that paper, so its exact statement is unconfirmed here and it is left out of the papers list.

**Off-target result:** Chase, Ito and Mehalel (COLT 2026) also came up. Their paper is about bandits with expert advice, a different problem.

Sources: [arXiv 1607.02834](https://export.arxiv.org/pdf/1607.02834), [Google Research page](https://research.google/pubs/tight-lower-bounds-for-multiplicative-weights-algorithmic-families/), [arXiv 1904.07272](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.07272)

Together with the Ω(sqrt(T log K)) minimax lower bound, this gives Θ(sqrt(T log K)) for full information.

triage.summary:
This gap is already closed by classical results. The minimax regret for the K-expert full-information problem with rewards in [0,1] is Θ(√(T log K)), and asymptotically it is exactly √((T/2) ln K).

**Upper bound.** Hedge (exponential weights) with learning rate η = √(8 ln K / T) gets regret at most √((T/2) ln K). This is the classical analysis by Freund–Schapire and Cesa-Bianchi et al. I did not fetch those original papers this session. Arxiv:2410.05124 states the order-√(T ln K) bound, and Gravin–Peres–Sivan (arXiv:1607.02834) state the exact constant.

**Lower bound.** Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi (2006), Theorem 7.4, uses i.i.d. Bernoulli(1/2) losses. As T and K go to infinity, any algorithm's regret is at least about √((T/2) ln K). I saw this through a summary in arXiv:2509.21547, not in the book itself. Arxiv:1910.13521 restates it, up to a constant, as min{√(2T log K), 2T}/L for a universal constant L.

**Why the database shows a gap.** Its upper bounds come from bandit algorithms (Tsallis-INF, √(KT)), which have a polynomial dependence on K. Its lower bound already has the √(T log K) form. Plugging in Hedge's √((T/2) ln K) upper bound removes the polynomial gap in both K and T. So the worst-case status should be "tight" at Θ(√(T log K)).

**The Δ entry.** The Δ-dependent lower bound (Ito 2021) is about the stochastically constrained / best-of-both-worlds regime, not the worst case. For that regime, the full-information literature also gives O(log K / Δ)-type upper bounds, for example decreasing-rate Hedge (Mourtada & Gaillard 2019). This session did not search for or verify that claim, so it is not in the paper list.

**Caveat on the exact constant.** The 1/2 constant is matched only asymptotically. I found no source with a non-asymptotic proof of the exact constant for every K and T.
